**H** (or **h**) is the eighth (number 8) [letter](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Letter "Letter") in the [English](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language") [alphabet](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphabet "Alphabet"). The uppercase letter for H name is "aitch" pronounced /eɪtʃ/ **H**

## Meanings for H

[[change](/w/index.php?title=H&veaction=edit&section=1 "Change section: Meanings for H") | [change source](/w/index.php?title=H&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section's source code: Meanings for H")]

* In [chemistry](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemistry "Chemistry"), H is the symbol for [hydrogen](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen "Hydrogen").
* In [music](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music "Music"), H is a [note](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Note_(music) "Note (music)") in the [German](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany") system, meaning "B natural".
* In [particle physics](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particle_physics "Particle physics"), H is the symbol for the [Higgs boson](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higgs_boson "Higgs boson").

# The Letter H | Alphabet A-Z | Jack Hartmann Alphabet Song
## Channel: Jack Hartmann Kids Music Channel (verified)
5.62M subscribers
1K likes

### Description
671,016 views
Posted: 2020-07-28
This Jack Hartmann's Alphabet A-Z series for the letter H h. Learn about the Letter H.
Learn that H is a consonant in the alphabet. Learn to recognize the upper and lowercase letter H, how to write the letter H and the sound that letter H makes.  This series incorporates the modalities of visual, auditory and kinesthetic learning while teaching about each letter of the alphabet. This song engages students to be active learners while learning about each letter to build body and brain connections.  Learn how to form the upper and lowercase H with Jack Hartmann's catchy rhymes. These rhymes are a wonderful mnemonic way to remember letter formation.  Learn the H sound and  words that begin with the H sound.   Let's Learn From A to Z  with the letter Hh. Let's Learn from a z with Jack Hartmann's alphabet song for H h. Learn the letter sound for H h. ABC song for h.

### Usage notes

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=h&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Usage notes")]

The UPA distinguishes glottal fricatives from glottal approximants. The voiceless and voiced fricatives ('spirants') are *[ȟ](/wiki/%C8%9F "ȟ")*, *[ᴤ](/wiki/%E1%B4%A4 "ᴤ")*, while the voiceless and voiced approximants ('semivowels') are ***h***, *[ɦ](/wiki/%C9%A6 "ɦ")*.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

The Finnish orthography using the Latin script was based on those of Swedish, German, and Latin, and was first used in the mid-16th century. No earlier script is known. ## Khiamniungan Naga

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=h&action=edit&section=150 "Edit section: Khiamniungan Naga")]

### Etymology

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=h&action=edit&section=151 "Edit section: Etymology")]

The [Khiamniungan Naga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patsho_Khiamniungan "w:Patsho Khiamniungan") language is presently written using the [Latin alphabet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patsho_Khiamniungan#Alphabet "w:Patsho Khiamniungan"). No indigenous or alternative script has been documented from earlier periods in the language's history. For a detailed description of the writing system's conventions including [*vowel*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patsho_Khiamniungan#Vowels "w:Patsho Khiamniungan") and [*Consonant*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patsho_Khiamniungan#Phonology "w:Patsho Khiamniungan") representation, [tone marking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patsho_Khiamniungan#Phonemic_tones "w:Patsho Khiamniungan") (such as the use of [*h*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patsho_Khiamniungan#Writing_system "w:Patsho Khiamniungan") for glottal, the letter *ü* is pronounced *ə*), and orthographic rules, see the Wikipedia article on the [Khiamniungan alphabet.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patsho_Khiamniungan "w:Patsho Khiamniungan")

### Letter

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/86/Latin_alphabet_Hh.svg/250px-Latin_alphabet_Hh.svg.png?utm_source=en.wiktionary.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](/wiki/File:Latin_alphabet_Hh.svg)

H

**h** (*lower case*, *[upper case](/wiki/Appendix:Capital_letter "Appendix:Capital letter")* **[H](/wiki/H#Latvian "H")**)

1. The twelfth [letter](/wiki/letter "letter") of the Latvian [alphabet](/wiki/alphabet "alphabet"), called *[hā](/wiki/h%C4%81#Latvian "hā")* and written in the [Latin script](/wiki/Appendix:Latin_script "Appendix:Latin script").

#### Usage notes

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=h&action=edit&section=163 "Edit section: Usage notes")]

The letter ***H***/***h*** (like ***F***/***f***, and ***O***/***o*** representing [o], [oː] instead of [uə̯]) is found only in words of foreign origin (borrowings). Note that it represents the sound of IPA [x] (like [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language "w:German language") *[machen](/wiki/machen#German "machen")*, *[ach](/wiki/ach#German "ach")*), not (as in most other alphabets based on the Latin script) the sound of IPA [h].

## Maltese

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=h&action=edit&section=181 "Edit section: Maltese")]

### Etymology

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=h&action=edit&section=182 "Edit section: Etymology")]

In pre-modern Maltese, ‘‘h’’ still represented the sound [h], as recorded by [Agius de Soldanis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giovanni_Pietro_Francesco_Agius_de_Soldanis "w:Giovanni Pietro Francesco Agius de Soldanis") (1750) and [Mikiel Anton Vassalli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikiel_Anton_Vassalli "w:Mikiel Anton Vassalli") (1796). The modern pronunciation first appeared in the dialect known as *lsien tal-bliet* (“tongues of the cities”, referring to the urban areas around the [Grand Harbour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Harbour "w:Grand Harbour") according to Vassalli), and eventually replaced the increasingly archaic [h] sound in the surrounding regions.

### Pronunciation

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=h&action=edit&section=183 "Edit section: Pronunciation")]

* (phoneme) [IPA](/wiki/Wiktionary:International_Phonetic_Alphabet "Wiktionary:International Phonetic Alphabet")([key](/wiki/Appendix:Maltese_pronunciation "Appendix:Maltese pronunciation")): /-/, /ː/, /j/, /w/, /ħ/

### Letter

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=h&action=edit&section=184 "Edit section: Letter")]

**h** (*lower case*, *[upper case](/wiki/Appendix:Capital_letter "Appendix:Capital letter")* **[H](/wiki/H#Maltese "H")**)

1. The tenth [letter](/wiki/letter "letter") of the Maltese [alphabet](/wiki/alphabet "alphabet"), written in the [Latin script](/wiki/Appendix:Latin_script "Appendix:Latin script").

#### Usage notes

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=h&action=edit&section=185 "Edit section: Usage notes")]

* In contemporary Maltese, *h* remains a true consonant [ħ] in the following cases:
  + in word-final position or when being the last radical of a verb: *[ikrah](/wiki/ikrah#Maltese "ikrah")* [ˈɪkraħ], *[jixbhu](/wiki/xebah#Maltese "xebah")* [ˈjɪʃpħʊ];
  + before the negative ending *[-x](/wiki/-x#Maltese "-x")*: *[jarawhx](/wiki/ra#Maltese "ra")* [jaˈrawħʃ];
  + in the clusters *-għh-, -ħh-*, *-hh-*, which all become [ħħ].
* Otherwise it is silent or leaves only a vocalic trace:
  + Following and preceding *a, e, o* are lengthened if stressed: *[hedded](/wiki/hedded#Maltese "hedded")* [ˈɛːddɛt], *[fehmet](/wiki/fehmet#Maltese "fehmet")* [ˈfɛːmɛt]. Other vowels are not affected.
  + In intervocalic position it is a glide, [j] after *i, ie*, and [w] after *u*: *jibniha* [jɪbˈnɪːja], *inħobbuhom* [ɪnħɔbˈbuːwɔm].
  + The sequence *-aho-* becomes [ɔː]: *rahom* [rɔːm]. The sequence *-ehi-* becomes [ɛj] or [ɛˈjiː]: *[ftehim](/wiki/ftehim#Maltese "ftehim")* [ftɛjm], [ftɛˈjiːm].
* Phonotactically, word-initial *h* now generally behaves like a vowel, allowing contractions such as *[m’](/wiki/ma#Maltese "ma")[hemm](/wiki/hemm#Maltese "hemm")[x](/wiki/-x#Maltese "-x")* [mɛːmʃ]. However, word-internal *h* still behaves like a (virtual) consonant. Compare for example *[qablu](/wiki/qablu#Maltese "qablu")* [ˈʔablʊ] with *[qabilha](/wiki/qabilha#Maltese "qabilha")* [ʔaˈbɪla], which latter is formed as though the *l* were followed by a consonant.

## Polish

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=h&action=edit&section=219 "Edit section: Polish")]

### Etymology 1

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=h&action=edit&section=220 "Edit section: Etymology 1")]

The Polish orthography is based on the Latin alphabet. No earlier script is known. See the [history of Polish orthography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Polish_orthography "w:History of Polish orthography") article on Wikipedia for more, and *[h](#Translingual)* for development of the glyph itself.

#### Pronunciation

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=h&action=edit&section=221 "Edit section: Pronunciation")]

* [IPA](/wiki/Wiktionary:International_Phonetic_Alphabet "Wiktionary:International Phonetic Alphabet")([key](/wiki/Appendix:Polish_pronunciation "Appendix:Polish pronunciation")): /ˈxa/

#### Letter

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=h&action=edit&section=222 "Edit section: Letter")]

**h** (*lower case*, *[upper case](/wiki/Appendix:Capital_letter "Appendix:Capital letter")* **[H](/wiki/H#Polish "H")**)

1. The eleventh [letter](/wiki/letter "letter") of the Polish [alphabet](/wiki/alphabet "alphabet"), called *[ha](/wiki/ha#Polish "ha")* and written in the [Latin script](/wiki/Appendix:Latin_script "Appendix:Latin script").

##### Usage notes

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=h&action=edit&section=223 "Edit section: Usage notes")]

* Seemingly native words spelt with ⟨h⟩, rather than ⟨ch⟩, are generally from [Czech](/wiki/Czech "Czech") or other Slavic dialects. Otherwise ⟨h⟩ occurs in non-Slavic loanwords, especially from Latin and German. Some dialects distinguish between /x/ and /h/, but this is not part of standard Polish.

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=h&action=edit&section=231 "Edit section: Letter")]

**h** m (*lower case*, *[upper case](/wiki/Appendix:Capital_letter "Appendix:Capital letter")* **[H](/wiki/H#Portuguese "H")**)

1. The eighth [letter](/wiki/letter "letter") of the Portuguese [alphabet](/wiki/alphabet "alphabet"), called *[agá](/wiki/ag%C3%A1#Portuguese "agá")* and written in the [Latin script](/wiki/Appendix:Latin_script "Appendix:Latin script").
   1. silent letter used mainly in words derived from Latin, Greek and other Romance languages; word-initial only

      2. ([obsolete](/wiki/Appendix:Glossary#obsolete "Appendix:Glossary") except in given names) used in the Hellenistic digraphs *th*, *ph* and *rh*

         :   *[thesouro](/wiki/thesouro#Portuguese "thesouro") (now [tesouro](/wiki/tesouro#Portuguese "tesouro")), [phalange](/wiki/phalange#Portuguese "phalange") (now [falange](/wiki/falange#Portuguese "falange")), [rheumatismo](/w/index.php?title=rheumatismo&action=edit&redlink=1 "rheumatismo (page does not exist)") (now [reumatismo](/wiki/reumatismo#Portuguese "reumatismo")), [Cynthia](/wiki/Cynthia#Portuguese "Cynthia") (alongside [Cíntia](/wiki/C%C3%ADntia#Portuguese "Cíntia"))* ― treasure, phalanx, rheumatism, Cynthia
      3. ([obsolete](/wiki/Appendix:Glossary#obsolete "Appendix:Glossary") except in given names) used in words perceived to be Hellenisms

         :   *[thesoura](/wiki/thesoura#Portuguese "thesoura") (now [tesoura](/wiki/tesoura#Portuguese "tesoura")), [Nathalia](/wiki/Nathalia#Portuguese "Nathalia")* ― scissors, Natalie
   2. represents /h/ in most recent loanwords from other languages, most commonly English

      :   *[hardcore](/wiki/hardcore#Portuguese "hardcore"), [hacker](/wiki/hacker#Portuguese "hacker"), [hall](/wiki/hall#Portuguese "hall")*

          :   hardcore punk, hacker, entry hall
   3. used in the digraphs *ch*, *lh* and *nh*, where it indicates a palatal or post-alveolar pronunciation

      :   *[cheio](/wiki/cheio#Portuguese "cheio"), [alho](/wiki/alho#Portuguese "alho"), [banho](/wiki/banho#Portuguese "banho")* ― full, garlic, bath
   4. ([obsolete](/wiki/Appendix:Glossary#obsolete "Appendix:Glossary")) silent letter used word-initially in monosyllabic verbs with no attack

      :   *[hir](/wiki/hir#Portuguese "hir") (now [ir](/wiki/ir#Portuguese "ir")), [he](/wiki/he#Portuguese "he") (now [é](/wiki/%C3%A9#Portuguese "é"))* ― to go, is
   5. silent letter used syllable-finally in some interjections

      :   *[ih](/wiki/ih#Portuguese "ih")! [oh](/wiki/oh#Portuguese "oh")!* ― uh oh! ooh!
   6. represents /h/ in some expressive terms

      :   *[hahaha](/wiki/hahaha#Portuguese "hahaha")! [aham](/wiki/aham#Portuguese "aham"), [hue hue](/w/index.php?title=hue_hue&action=edit&redlink=1 "hue hue (page does not exist)")* ― hahaha! yep, hehehe
   7. (chiefly [Internet](/wiki/Internet "Internet") [slang](/wiki/Appendix:Glossary#slang "Appendix:Glossary")) used as a replacement for the acute or circumflex accent, or silent infinitive -r, indicating stress

      :   *[sahir](/wiki/sahir#Portuguese "sahir") (now [sair](/wiki/sair#Portuguese "sair")), [bahia](/wiki/bahia#Portuguese "bahia") (now [baía](/wiki/ba%C3%ADa#Portuguese "baía"))*

   2. used to indicate any sequence of time in hours

      :   *O atleta completou a corrida em 1h20[min](/wiki/min#Portuguese "min")45[s](/wiki/s#Portuguese "s")* ― The athlete completed the race in 1 hour, 21 minutes and 45 seconds

#### Usage notes

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=h&action=edit&section=234 "Edit section: Usage notes")]

* This abbreviation uses no spaces or points and must always follow a number (in its most common usage, a number between 0 and 23 to indicate the day's hours).
* The abbreviation can be followed by a number between 00 and 59 to indicate the minutes of an hour (as in French). This can be optionally represented by another abbreviation: *[min](/wiki/min#Portuguese "min")*.
  + Example: *15h30* or *15h30min*, the first being much more common
* *[min](/wiki/min#Portuguese "min")* can be further followed by another abbreviation, *[s](/wiki/s#Portuguese "s")*, to represent seconds.
  + Example: *20h43min08s*

### Etymology 1

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=h&action=edit&section=264 "Edit section: Etymology 1")]

From Gaj's Latin alphabet *[h](#Serbo-Croatian)*, from [Czech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czech_language "w:Czech language") alphabet *[h](#Czech)*, from Latin *[h](#Latin)*. Pronunciation as /xə/ is initial Slovene (phoneme plus a fill vowel) and the second pronunciation is probably taken from [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language "w:German language") *[h](#German)*.

##### Usage notes

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=h&action=edit&section=267 "Edit section: Usage notes")]

In Metelko alphabet, the phoneme was written by two different letters whether it was pronounced as velar /x/ or glottal /h/, a distinction irrelevant to nowadays standard and the distinction was also not used by all writers. Phoneme /h/ was written with 〈h〉, while /x/ was written with a yet to be encoded character [![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/6e/Metelko_h.gif?utm_source=en.wiktionary.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](/wiki/File:Metelko_h.gif).

### Etymology 2

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=h&action=edit&section=271 "Edit section: Etymology 2")]

From [Proto-Slavic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Slavic_language "w:Proto-Slavic language") *[\*kъ](/wiki/Reconstruction:Proto-Slavic/k%D1%8A "Reconstruction:Proto-Slavic/kъ")* 'to', which is itself probably from [Proto-Indo-European](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Indo-European_language "w:Proto-Indo-European language") *[\*kwu](/w/index.php?title=Reconstruction:Proto-Indo-European/kwu&action=edit&redlink=1 "Reconstruction:Proto-Indo-European/kwu (page does not exist)")* 'where'. This form is a [spirantization](/wiki/spirantization "spirantization") of [k](/wiki/k#Slovene "k"), which appeared to ease the pronunciation.

#### Preposition

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=h&action=edit&section=273 "Edit section: Preposition")]

**h**

1. (with dative, see usage notes) [to](/wiki/to "to"), [for](/wiki/for "for")

##### Usage notes

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=h&action=edit&section=274 "Edit section: Usage notes")]

Preposition *h* is a form of preposition [k](/wiki/k#Slovene "k") that appears before words that start with /k/ or /ɡ/ while other form is used for all other words. In "correct" pronunciation, the preposition does not form its own syllable, but binds to the first syllable of the next word and has therefore two pronunciations: [x] if word starts with [k] and [ɣ] if word starts with [ɡ]. In colloquial speech, this form (or at least its pronunciation) are also used with words starting with other letters.

**H** ([minuscule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Letter_case "Letter case"): **h**) is the eighth [letter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Letter_(alphabet) "Letter (alphabet)") of the [Latin alphabet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_alphabet "Latin alphabet"), used in the [modern English alphabet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_alphabet "English alphabet"), including the alphabets of other Western European languages and others worldwide. Its name in English is [*aitch*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_alphabet#Letter_names "English alphabet") (pronounced [/eɪtʃ/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English") [ⓘ](/wiki/File:LL-Q1860_(eng)-Flame,_not_lame-H.wav "File:LL-Q1860 (eng)-Flame, not lame-H.wav"), plural *aitches*), or regionally *haitch* (pronounced [/heɪtʃ/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"), plural *haitches*)*.*[[1]](#cite_note-mw-1)

## Name

### English

For most English speakers, the name for the letter is pronounced as [/eɪtʃ/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English") and spelled "aitch"[[1]](#cite_note-mw-1) or occasionally "eitch". The pronunciation [/heɪtʃ/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English") and the associated spelling "haitch" are often considered to be [h-adding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H-dropping#H-insertion "H-dropping") and are considered non-standard in England.[[2]](#cite_note-how_do_you_pronounce_H-2) It is, however, a feature of [Hiberno-English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiberno-English "Hiberno-English"),[[3]](#cite_note-3) and occurs sporadically in various other dialects.

The perceived name of the letter affects the choice of [indefinite article](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_and_an "A and an") before [initialisms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initialism "Initialism") beginning with H: for example "an H-bomb" or "a H-bomb". The pronunciation /heɪtʃ/ may be a [hypercorrection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypercorrection "Hypercorrection") formed by analogy with the names of the other letters of the alphabet, most of which include the sound they represent.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

The *haitch* pronunciation of *h* has spread in England, being used by approximately 24% of English people born since 1982,[[5]](#cite_note-5) and polls continue to show this pronunciation becoming more common among younger native speakers. Despite this increasing number, the pronunciation without the /h/ sound is still considered standard in England, although the pronunciation with /h/ is also attested as a legitimate variant.[[2]](#cite_note-how_do_you_pronounce_H-2) In [Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland "Northern Ireland"), the pronunciation of the letter has been used as a [shibboleth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shibboleth "Shibboleth"), with Catholics typically pronouncing it with the /h/ and Protestants pronouncing the letter without it.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Authorities disagree about the history of the letter's name. The *[Oxford English Dictionary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_English_Dictionary "Oxford English Dictionary")* says the original name of the letter was [[ˈaha]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Latin "Help:IPA/Latin") in Latin; this became [[ˈaka]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Latin "Help:IPA/Latin") in Vulgar Latin, passed into English via Old French [[atʃ]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Old_English "Help:IPA/Old English"), and by Middle English was pronounced [[aːtʃ]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA "Help:IPA"). *[The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_American_Heritage_Dictionary_of_the_English_Language "The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language")* derives it from French *hache* from Latin *haca* or *hic*. [Anatoly Liberman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatoly_Liberman "Anatoly Liberman") suggests a conflation of two obsolete orderings of the alphabet, one with *H* immediately followed by *K* and the other without any *K*: reciting the former's *..., H, K, L,...* as [...(h)a ka el ...] when reinterpreted for the latter *..., H, L,...* would imply a pronunciation of [(h)a ka] for *H*.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

The original [Semitic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semitic_languages "Semitic languages") letter [Heth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heth "Heth") most likely represented the [voiceless pharyngeal fricative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_pharyngeal_fricative "Voiceless pharyngeal fricative") ([ħ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_pharyngeal_fricative "Voiceless pharyngeal fricative")). The form of the letter probably stood for a fence or post.

The [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_alphabet "Greek alphabet") [Eta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eta_(letter) "Eta (letter)") 'Η' in [archaic Greek alphabets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaic_Greek_alphabets#Eta_and_/h/ "Archaic Greek alphabets"), before coming to represent a long vowel, /ɛː/, still represented a similar sound, the [voiceless glottal fricative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_glottal_fricative "Voiceless glottal fricative") /h/. In this context, the letter eta is also known as *[Heta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heta "Heta")*. Thus, in the [Old Italic alphabets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Italic_alphabets "Old Italic alphabets"), the letter Heta of the [Euboean alphabet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euboean_alphabet "Euboean alphabet") was adopted with its original sound value /h/.

While [Etruscan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etruscan_language "Etruscan language") and [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin "Latin") had /h/ as a [phoneme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoneme "Phoneme"), almost all [Romance languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romance_languages "Romance languages") lost the sound—[Romanian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_language "Romanian language") later re-borrowed the /h/ phoneme from its neighbouring Slavic languages, and [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language") developed a secondary /h/ from /f/, before losing it again; various Spanish dialects have developed [h] as an [allophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allophone "Allophone") of /s/ or /x/ in most Spanish-speaking countries, and various dialects of [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_language "Portuguese language") use it as an allophone of /ʁ/. 'H' is also used in many spelling systems in [digraphs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digraph_(orthography) "Digraph (orthography)") and [trigraphs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigraph_(orthography) "Trigraph (orthography)"), such as 'ch', which represents /tʃ/ in Spanish, [Galician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galician_language "Galician language"), and [Old Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Portuguese "Old Portuguese"); /ʃ/ in [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language") and [modern Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_Portuguese "Modern Portuguese"); /k/ in [Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_language "Italian language") and French.

### English

In English, ⟨h⟩ occurs as a single-letter [grapheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grapheme "Grapheme") (being either [silent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silent_letter "Silent letter") or representing the [voiceless glottal fricative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_glottal_fricative "Voiceless glottal fricative") /[h](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_glottal_fricative "Voiceless glottal fricative")/ and in various [digraphs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digraph_(orthography) "Digraph (orthography)"):

* ⟨ch⟩ representing /[tʃ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_postalveolar_affricate "Voiceless postalveolar affricate")/, /[ʃ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_postalveolar_fricative "Voiceless postalveolar fricative")/, /[k](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_velar_plosive "Voiceless velar plosive")/, or /[x](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_velar_fricative "Voiceless velar fricative")/
* ⟨gh⟩ being silent or representing /[ɡ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiced_velar_plosive "Voiced velar plosive")/, /[k](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_velar_plosive "Voiceless velar plosive")/, /[p](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_bilabial_plosive "Voiceless bilabial plosive")/, or /[f](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_labiodental_fricative "Voiceless labiodental fricative")/
* ⟨ph⟩ representing /[f](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_labiodental_fricative "Voiceless labiodental fricative")/
* ⟨rh⟩ representing /[r](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiced_alveolar_trill "Voiced alveolar trill")/
* ⟨sh⟩ representing /[ʃ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_postalveolar_fricative "Voiceless postalveolar fricative")/
* ⟨th⟩ representing /[θ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_dental_fricative "Voiceless dental fricative")/ or /[ð](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiced_dental_fricative "Voiced dental fricative")/
* ⟨wh⟩ representing /[hw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_labial–velar_fricative "Voiceless labial–velar fricative")/[[8]](#cite_note-8) or /[h](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_glottal_fricative "Voiceless glottal fricative")/

The letter is silent in a [syllable rime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syllable_rime "Syllable rime"), as in *ah*, *ohm*, *dahlia*, *cheetah*, and *pooh-poohed*, as well as in certain other words (mostly of French origin) such as *hour*, *honest*, *herb*, and *vehicle* (in [American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_English "American English") but not [British English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_English "British English")). Initial /h/ is often not pronounced in the [weak form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weak_and_strong_forms_in_English "Weak and strong forms in English") of some [function words](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_word "Function word"), including *had*, *has*, *have*, *he*, *her*, *him*, *his*, and in some varieties of English (including most regional dialects of England and Wales), it is often [omitted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H-dropping "H-dropping") in all words. It was formerly common for *an* rather than *a* to be used as the indefinite article before a word beginning with /h/ in an [unstressed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stress_(linguistics) "Stress (linguistics)") syllable, as in "an historian", but the use of *a* is now more usual.

In English, the pronunciation of ⟨h⟩ as /h/ can be analyzed as a voiceless vowel. That is, when the phoneme /h/ precedes a vowel, /h/ may be realized as a voiceless version of the subsequent vowel. For example, the word ⟨hit⟩, /hɪt/ is realized as [ɪ̥ɪt].[[9]](#cite_note-9)

H is the [eighth most frequently used letter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Letter_frequency "Letter frequency") in the English language (after [S](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S "S"), [N](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N "N"), [I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I "I"), [O](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O "O"), [A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A "A"), [T](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T "T"), and [E](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E "E")), with a frequency of about 6.1% in words.[[10]](#cite_note-micka-10)

### Other languages

In [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language "German language"), following a vowel, it often silently indicates that the vowel is long: In the word *erhöhen* ('heighten'), the second ⟨h⟩ is mute for most speakers outside of Switzerland. In 1901, a [spelling reform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spelling_reform "Spelling reform") eliminated the silent ⟨h⟩ in nearly all instances of ⟨th⟩ in native German words such as *thun* ('to do') or *Thür* ('door'). It has been left unchanged in words derived from Greek, such as *Theater* ('theater') and *Thron* ('throne'), which continue to be spelled with ⟨th⟩ even after the last German spelling reform.

In [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language") and [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_language "Portuguese language"), ⟨h⟩ is a silent letter with no pronunciation, as in *hijo* [[ˈixo]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish") ('son') and *húngaro* [[ˈũɡaɾu]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Portuguese "Help:IPA/Portuguese") ('Hungarian'). The spelling reflects an earlier pronunciation of the sound /h/. In words where the ⟨h⟩ is derived from a Latin /f/, it is still sometimes pronounced with the value [h] in some regions of [Andalusia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andalusia "Andalusia"), [Extremadura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extremadura "Extremadura"), [Canarias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands "Canary Islands"), [Cantabria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantabria "Cantabria"), and the Americas. Some words beginning with [je] or [we], such as *hielo*, 'ice' and *huevo*, 'egg', were given an initial ⟨h⟩ to avoid confusion between their initial semivowels and the consonants ⟨j⟩ and ⟨v⟩. This is because ⟨j⟩ and ⟨v⟩ used to be considered variants of ⟨i⟩ and ⟨u⟩ respectively. ⟨h⟩ also appears in the digraph ⟨ch⟩, which represents /[tʃ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_postalveolar_affricate "Voiceless postalveolar affricate")/ in Spanish and northern Portugal, and /[ʃ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_postalveolar_fricative "Voiceless postalveolar fricative")/ in varieties that have merged both sounds (the latter originally represented by ⟨x⟩ instead), such as most of the Portuguese language and some Spanish dialects, prominently [Chilean Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chilean_Spanish "Chilean Spanish").

[French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language") orthography classifies words that begin with this letter in two ways, one of which can affect the pronunciation, even though it is a silent letter either way. The *H muet*, or "mute" ⟨h⟩, is considered as though the letter were not there at all. For example, the singular definite [article](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Article_(grammar) "Article (grammar)") *le* or *la*, which is [elided](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elision_(French) "Elision (French)") to *l'* before a vowel, elides before an *H muet* followed by a vowel. For example, *le + hébergement* becomes *l'hébergement* ('the accommodation'). The other kind of ⟨h⟩ is called *h aspiré* ("[aspirated '⟨h⟩'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aspirated_h "Aspirated h")", though it is not normally aspirated phonetically), and does not allow elision or [liaison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liaison_(French) "Liaison (French)"). For example, in *le homard* ('the lobster') the article *le* remains unelided, and may be separated from the noun with a bit of a glottal stop. Most words that begin with an *H muet* come from Latin (*honneur*, *homme*) or from Greek through Latin (*hécatombe*), whereas most words beginning with an *H aspiré* come from Germanic (*harpe*, *hareng*) or non-Indo-European languages (*harem*, *hamac*, *haricot*); in some cases, an orthographic ⟨h⟩ was added to disambiguate the [v] and semivowel [ɥ] pronunciations before the introduction of the distinction between the letters ⟨v⟩ and ⟨u⟩: *huit* (from *uit*, ultimately from Latin *octo*), *huître* (from *uistre*, ultimately from Greek through Latin *ostrea*).

In Italian, ⟨h⟩ has no [phonological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phonology "Phonology") value. Its most important uses are in the [digraphs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digraph_(orthography) "Digraph (orthography)") 'ch' /k/ and 'gh' /ɡ/, as well as to differentiate the spellings of certain short words that are [homophones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homophone "Homophone"), for example, some [present tense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Present_tense "Present tense") forms of the verb *avere* ('to have') (such as *hanno*, 'they have', vs. *anno*, 'year'), and in short [interjections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interjection "Interjection") (*oh*, *ehi*).

Some languages, including [Czech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czech_language "Czech language"), [Slovak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovak_language "Slovak language"), [Hungarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_language "Hungarian language"), [Finnish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_language "Finnish language"), and [Estonian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estonian_language "Estonian language"), use ⟨h⟩ as a [breathy voiced glottal fricative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiced_glottal_fricative "Voiced glottal fricative") [ɦ], often as an allophone of otherwise voiceless /h/ in a voiced environment.

In [Hungarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_phonology "Hungarian phonology"), the letter represents a phoneme /[h](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_glottal_fricative "Voiceless glottal fricative")/ with four allophones: [[h](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_glottal_fricative "Voiceless glottal fricative")] before vowels, [[ɦ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiced_glottal_fricative "Voiced glottal fricative")] between two vowels, [[ç](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_palatal_fricative "Voiceless palatal fricative")] after [front vowels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Front_vowel "Front vowel"), and [[x](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_velar_fricative "Voiceless velar fricative")] word-finally after [back vowels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back_vowel "Back vowel"). It can also be a silent word-finally after back vowels. It is [[xː](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_velar_fricative "Voiceless velar fricative")] when geminated. In archaic spelling, the digraph ⟨ch⟩ represents /[t͡ʃ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_postalveolar_affricate "Voiceless postalveolar affricate")/ (as in the name *[Széchenyi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/István_Széchenyi "István Széchenyi")*) and /[h](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_glottal_fricative "Voiceless glottal fricative")/ (as in *[pech](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/pech#Hungarian "wikt:pech")*, which is pronounced [pɛxː]); in certain environments it breaks palatalization of a consonant, as in the name *Beöthy*, which is pronounced [bøːti] (without the intervening *h,* the name *Beöty* could be pronounced [bøːc]); and finally, it acts as a silent component of a digraph, as in the name *Vargha,* pronounced [vɒrgɒ].

In [Ukrainian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukrainian_language "Ukrainian language") and [Belarusian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belarusian_language "Belarusian language"), when written in the Latin alphabet, ⟨h⟩ is also commonly used for /ɦ/, which is otherwise written with the Cyrillic letter ⟨г⟩.

In [Irish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_language "Irish language"), ⟨h⟩ is not considered an independent letter, except for a very few non-native words; however, ⟨h⟩ placed after a consonant is known as a "séimhiú" and indicates the [lenition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenition "Lenition") of that consonant; ⟨h⟩ began to replace the original form of a séimhiú, a dot placed above the consonant, after the introduction of typewriters.

In most dialects of Polish, both ⟨h⟩ and the digraph ⟨ch⟩ always represent /x/.

In [Basque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basque_language "Basque language"), during the 20th century, it was not used in the orthography of the Basque dialects in Spain but it marked an aspiration in the North-Eastern dialects. During the [standardization of Basque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Basque "Standard Basque") in the 1970s, a compromise was reached that *h* would be accepted if it were the first consonant in a syllable. Hence, *herri* ("people") and *etorri* ("to come") were accepted instead of *erri* ([Biscayan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biscayan_Basque "Biscayan Basque")) and *ethorri* ([Souletin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Souletin "Souletin")).

### Other systems

As a phonetic symbol in the [International Phonetic Alphabet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Phonetic_Alphabet "International Phonetic Alphabet") (IPA), it is used mainly for the so-called aspirations (fricative or trills), and variations of the plain letter are used to represent two sounds: the lowercase form ⟨[h](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_glottal_fricative "Voiceless glottal fricative")⟩ represents the [voiceless glottal fricative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_glottal_fricative "Voiceless glottal fricative"), and the small capital form ⟨[ʜ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_epiglottal_trill "Voiceless epiglottal trill")⟩ represents the [voiceless epiglottal fricative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_epiglottal_fricative "Voiceless epiglottal fricative") (or trill). With a bar, minuscule ⟨[ħ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_pharyngeal_fricative "Voiceless pharyngeal fricative")⟩ is used for a [voiceless pharyngeal fricative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_pharyngeal_fricative "Voiceless pharyngeal fricative"). Specific to the IPA, a hooked ⟨[ɦ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiced_glottal_fricative "Voiced glottal fricative")⟩ is used for a [voiced glottal fricative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiced_glottal_fricative "Voiced glottal fricative"), and a superscript ⟨[ʰ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aspirated_consonant "Aspirated consonant")⟩ is used to represent [aspiration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aspiration_(phonetics) "Aspiration (phonetics)").

* H with [diacritics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diacritic "Diacritic"): [Ĥ ĥ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ĥ "Ĥ") [Ȟ ȟ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ȟ "Ȟ") [Ħ ħ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ħ "Ħ") [Ḩ ḩ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedilla "Cedilla") [Ⱨ ⱨ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ⱨ "Ⱨ") [ẖ ẖ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macron_(diacritic) "Macron (diacritic)") [Ḥ ḥ Ḣ ḣ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dot_(diacritic) "Dot (diacritic)") [Ḧ ḧ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ḧ "Ḧ") [Ḫ ḫ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ḫ "Ḫ") [ꞕ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ꞕ "ꞕ") [Ꜧ ꜧ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heng_(letter) "Heng (letter)")
* [IPA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Phonetic_Alphabet "International Phonetic Alphabet")-specific symbols related to H: [ʜ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_epiglottal_trill "Voiceless epiglottal trill") [ɦ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiced_glottal_fricative "Voiced glottal fricative") [ʰ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aspirated_consonant "Aspirated consonant") [ʱ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breathy_voice "Breathy voice") [ɥ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiced_labial–palatal_approximant "Voiced labial–palatal approximant") [ᶣ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labio-palatalization "Labio-palatalization")[[11]](#cite_note-11) [ɧ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sj-sound "Sj-sound")
* [Superscript IPA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Phonetic_Alphabet#Superscript_IPA "International Phonetic Alphabet") symbols related to H:[[12]](#cite_note-L220252-12) 𐞖 𐞕
* [ꟸ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ꟸ "ꟸ"): Modifier letter capital H with stroke is used in [VoQS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VoQS "VoQS") to represent [faucalized voice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faucalized_voice "Faucalized voice").
* ᴴ : Modifier letter H is used in the [Uralic Phonetic Alphabet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uralic_Phonetic_Alphabet "Uralic Phonetic Alphabet")[[13]](#cite_note-13)
* ₕ : Subscript small h was used in the Uralic Phonetic Alphabet prior to its formal standardization in 1902[[14]](#cite_note-14)
* ʰ : Modifier letter small h is used in [Indo-European studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indo-European_studies "Indo-European studies")[[15]](#cite_note-15)
* [ʮ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ʮ "ʮ") and [ʯ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ʯ "ʯ") : Turned H with fishhook and turned H with fishhook and tail are used in Sino-Tibetanist linguistics[[16]](#cite_note-16)
* Ƕ ƕ : Latin letter [hwair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hwair "Hwair"), derived from a ligature of the digraph hv, and used to transliterate the [Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_alphabet "Gothic alphabet") letter 𐍈 (which represented the sound [hʷ])
* Ⱶ ⱶ : [Claudian letters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudian_letters "Claudian letters")[[17]](#cite_note-17)
* Ꟶ ꟶ : Reversed half h used in Roman inscriptions from the Roman provinces of Gaul[[18]](#cite_note-18)

[*h*](https://cdn.britannica.com/94/67694-004-FB8EC1C1/letter-History-picture-sign-fence-eta-H-1000-bce.jpg)
History of the letter *h*. The letter *H* may have started as a picture sign of a fence, as in very early Semitic writing used about 1500 bce on the Sinai Peninsula (1). About 1000 bce, in Byblos and other Phoenician and Canaanite centres, the sign was given a linear form (2), the source of all later forms. The sign was called *cheth* in the Semitic languages, which may have meant “fence.” The sound expressed by the *cheth* sign stood for a pharyngeal sound which is not found in the English language. The Greeks renamed the sign *eta* and used it in two functions—first for the consonant *h* and then for the long vowel *e* (3). The Romans took over the form *H* (4), with the sound value of the English *h*. From Latin the capital letter came into English unchanged. A small Greek *eta* with curves (5) was developed from the capital letter. By the 9th century the corresponding Latin letter acquired a shape (6) much like the English handwritten and printed small *h*.

[History](https://www.britannica.com/topic/H-letter/additional-info#history)

**h**, eighth letter of the [alphabet](https://www.britannica.com/topic/alphabet-writing). It corresponds to [Semitic](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Semitic-languages) *cheth* and [Greek](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Greek-alphabet) *eta* (Η). It may derive from an early symbol for fence. In the early Greek alphabets a form with three horizontal bars and the simpler form *H* were both widely distributed. In [Etruscan](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Etruscan-alphabet) the prevailing form was similar to the early Greek form, and the same or a similar form occurs in very early [Latin](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Latin-alphabet) inscriptions, but the form *H* came into general use in Latin, either from the Chalcidic Greek alphabet of [Cumae](https://www.britannica.com/place/Cumae) or from some other source. The modern majuscule *H* is derived directly from the Latin. The cursive Latin form resembled a stylized version of the modern minuscule *h*, as did the [uncial](https://www.britannica.com/topic/uncial) form. Both of these forms result from writing the letter without taking the pen from the paper, the right-hand vertical bar being thus foreshortened and the horizontal stroke rounded. From these came the [Carolingian](https://www.britannica.com/art/Carolingian-minuscule) form as well as the modern minuscule *h*.

In the alphabets used to write the East Ionic dialect of Greek the letter became superfluous as a result of the disappearance of the [aspirate](https://www.britannica.com/topic/aspirate) which it represented in that dialect. It was accordingly put to a new use to indicate the open long *e* which had arisen through alteration of the primitive Greek long *a*. In a few inscriptions from [Thera](https://www.britannica.com/place/Thera), [Naxos](https://www.britannica.com/place/Naxos-ancient-Greek-colony-Sicily), and several other localities the letter was used with syllabic value; that is, it included *he*, thus showing its old consonantal and its new vocalic value at the same time. Eventually, as a result of the spread of the [Ionic alphabet](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Ionic-alphabet), its use for the long vowel *e* or η became general throughout Greece, while its consonantal value as the aspirate *h* passed from the western Greek alphabets into the Etruscan alphabets and then into the Latin and other alphabets of ancient Italy. In the [Romance languages](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Romance-languages) the sound has largely disappeared, but the letter is still extensively used, partly with only etymological value, (e.g., French *homme*), partly with fancied etymological value (e.g., French *haut* from Latin *altus*, with *h* through the influence of *hoh*, the [Old High German](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Old-High-German) word of the same meaning), partly with special orthographical functions. For example, in Italian *h* is used in combination with *c* or *g* to indicate the hard sound before a front vowel (e.g., *chi*, *ghetto*).

In English the initial *h* is pronounced in words of Germanic origin (e.g., *hunt*, *hook*); in some words of Romance origin, the h remains unpronounced (e.g., *heir*, *honour*), but in others it has been restored (e.g., *humble*, *humour*). The initial *h* often disappears in unaccented syllables (e.g., “What did he say?”). In chemistry H is the symbol for the element [hydrogen](https://www.britannica.com/science/hydrogen).

Top Questions

### What is an alphabet?

An alphabet is a set of graphs or characters used to represent the phonemic structure of a language. In most alphabets, the characters are arranged in a definite order or sequence (e.g., A, B, C, etc.).

### Where does the word alphabet come from?

The word *alphabet* comes from the first two letters of the Greek alphabet: alpha and beta. It was first used, in its Latin form, *alphabetum*, by Tertullian during the 2nd–3rd century CE and by St. Jerome. The Classical Greeks customarily used the plural of *to gramma* (“the letter”); the later form *alphabētos* was probably adopted under Latin influence.

### How many letters are there in the Hebrew alphabet?

The Hebrew alphabet consists of 22 letters. All are consonants, though four of them (*alef*, *he*, *waw*, and *yod*) are also employed to represent long vowels.

### When was the Arabic alphabet developed?

The Arabic alphabet probably originated some time in the 4th century CE, but the earliest known extant Arabic writing is a trilingual inscription—Greek-Syriac-Arabic—dating 512 CE.

### When was the Latin-Turkish alphabet introduced?

The Latin-Turkish alphabet was introduced in 1928 and became general throughout Turkey in 1930. It contains 29 letters, of which two vowels (ö and ü) and three consonants (ç, ĝ, and ş) are distinguished by diacritical marks. In one distinction, the dot from i is eliminated (ı) to represent a new sound.

**alphabet**, set of graphs, or characters, used to represent the [phonemic](https://www.britannica.com/science/phonetics) structure of a [language](https://www.britannica.com/topic/language). In most alphabets the characters are arranged in a definite order, or sequence (e.g., A, B, C, etc.).

In the usual case, each alphabetic character represents either a [consonant](https://www.britannica.com/topic/consonant) or a [vowel](https://www.britannica.com/topic/vowel) rather than a [syllable](https://www.britannica.com/topic/syllable) or a group of [consonants](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/consonants) and vowels. As a result, the number of characters required can be held to a relative few. A language that has 30 consonant sounds and five vowels, for example, needs at most only 35 separate letters. In a [syllabary](https://www.britannica.com/topic/syllabary), on the other hand, the same language would require 30 × 5 symbols to represent each possible consonant-vowel syllable (e.g., separate forms for *ba*, *be*, *bi*, *bo*, *bu*; *da*, *de*, *di*; and so on) and an additional five symbols for the vowels, thereby making a total of 155 individual characters. Both syllabaries and alphabets are phonographic symbolizations; that is, they represent the sounds of words rather than units of meaning.

The word *alphabet*, from the first two letters of the Greek alphabet—*alpha* and *beta*—was first used, in its Latin form, *alphabetum*, by [Tertullian](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Tertullian) (2nd–3rd century ce), a Latin [ecclesiastical](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/ecclesiastical) writer and [Church Father](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Church-Father), and by [St. Jerome](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Saint-Jerome). The Classical Greeks customarily used the plural of *to gramma* (“the letter”); the later form *alphabētos* was probably adopted under Latin influence.

## Theories of the origin of the alphabet

[![The letters A, B, and C appear in white lettering on a green chalkboard background superimposed with a world map.](https://cdn.britannica.com/49/274049-138-B8742305/what-is-the-origin-of-the-latin-alphabet.jpg?w=800&h=450&c=crop)](/video/what-is-the-origin-of-the-latin-alphabet/-356612)

Why We All Use the Latin AlphabetEnglish and Czech and Swahili, oh my!

[See all videos for this article](/topic/alphabet-writing/images-videos)

The evolution of the alphabet involved two important achievements. The first was the step taken by a group of [Semitic-speaking](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Semitic-languages) people, perhaps the Phoenicians, on the eastern shore of the Mediterranean between 1700 and 1500 bce. This was the invention of a consonantal writing system known as [North Semitic](https://www.britannica.com/topic/North-Semitic-alphabet). The second was the invention, by the [Greeks](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Greek-alphabet), of characters for representing vowels. This step occurred between 800 and 700 bce. While some scholars consider the Semitic writing system an unvocalized syllabary and the Greek system the true alphabet, both are treated here as forms of the alphabet.

Over the centuries, various theories have been advanced to explain the origin of [alphabetic writing](https://www.britannica.com/topic/alphabetic-writing), and, since Classical times, the problem has been a matter of serious study. The Greeks and Romans considered five different peoples as the possible inventors of the alphabet—the Phoenicians, Egyptians, Assyrians, Cretans, and Hebrews. Among modern theories are some that are not very different from those of ancient days. Every country situated in or more or less near the eastern Mediterranean has been singled out for the honour. [Egyptian writing](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Egyptian-language#ref75139), [cuneiform](https://www.britannica.com/topic/cuneiform), Cretan, hieroglyphic Hittite, the [Cypriot syllabary](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Cypriot-syllabary), and other scripts have all been called [prototypes](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/prototypes) of the alphabet. The Egyptian theory actually subdivides into three separate theories, according to whether the Egyptian hieroglyphic, the hieratic, or the [demotic script](https://www.britannica.com/topic/demotic-script) is regarded as the true parent of alphabetic writing. Similarly, the idea that cuneiform was the [precursor](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/precursor) of the alphabet may also be subdivided into those singling out Sumerian, Babylonian, or Assyrian cuneiform.

[![Buddhist engravings on wall in Thailand. Hands on wall. Hompepage blog 2009, history and society, science and technology, geography and travel, explore discovery](https://cdn.britannica.com/62/129562-131-63F782C3/wall-engravings-Buddhist-Thailand-Hands-society-history-2009.jpg)

Britannica Quiz

Languages & Alphabets](/quiz/languages-alphabets)

Among the various other theories concerning the alphabet are the [hypotheses](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/hypotheses) that the alphabet was taken by the Philistines from Crete to Palestine, that the various ancient scripts of the Mediterranean countries developed from prehistoric geometric symbols employed throughout the Mediterranean area from the earliest times, and that the proto-Sinaitic inscriptions (discovered since 1905 in the [Sinai Peninsula](https://www.britannica.com/place/Sinai-Peninsula)) represent a stage of writing intermediate between the Egyptian hieroglyphics and the North Semitic alphabet. Another [hypothesis](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/hypothesis), the [Ugaritic](https://www.britannica.com/place/Ugarit) theory, evolved after an epoch-making discovery in 1929 (and the years following) at the site of the ancient [Ugarit](https://www.britannica.com/place/Ugarit), on the Syrian coast opposite the most easterly cape of Cyprus. Thousands of clay tablets were found there, documents of inestimable value in many fields of research (including [epigraphy](https://www.britannica.com/topic/epigraphy), [philology](https://www.britannica.com/science/philology), and the history of religion). Dating from the 15th and 14th centuries bce, they were written in a cuneiform alphabet of 30 letters.

The Early [Canaanite](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Canaanite-inscriptions) theory is based on several undeciphered inscriptions also discovered since 1929 at various [Palestinian](https://www.britannica.com/art/Syro-Palestinian-art) sites; the writings belong in part to *c.* 1700 bce and are thus the earliest preserved documents in an alphabetic writing.

Explore Britannica Premium!

The trusted destination for professionals, college students, and lifelong learners.

[SUBSCRIBE](https://premium.britannica.com/premium-membership/?utm_source=premium&utm_medium=inline-cta&utm_campaign=redesign-2026)

![Penguin, ship, mountain, atlas](https://cdn.britannica.com/marketing/inline-left.webp)

![shohei ohtani, plants, andy wharhol art](https://cdn.britannica.com/marketing/inline-right.webp)

![Mobile](https://cdn.britannica.com/marketing/inline-mobile.webp?w=400)

Despite the conflict in theories, scholars are generally agreed that, for about 200 years before the middle of the 2nd millennium bce, alphabet making was in the air in the Syro-Palestinian region. It is idle to speculate on the meaning of the various discoveries referred to. That they [manifest](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/manifest) closely related efforts is certain; what the exact relationship among these efforts was, and what their relationship with the North Semitic alphabet was, cannot be said with certainty.

It can, however, be [ascertained](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/ascertained) that the period from 1730 to 1580 bce in [Syria](https://www.britannica.com/place/Syria), Palestine, and Egypt, during which there was an uprooting of established cultural and ethnic patterns in the [Fertile Crescent](https://www.britannica.com/place/Fertile-Crescent), provided conditions favourable to the [conception](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/conception) of an alphabetic script, a kind of writing that would be more accessible to larger groups of people, in contrast to the scripts of the old states of Mesopotamia and Egypt, which were confined largely to the priestly class. In [default](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/default) of other direct evidence, it is reasonable to suppose that the actual [prototype](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/prototype) of the alphabet was not very different from the writing of the earliest North Semitic inscriptions now [extant](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/extant), which belong to the last two or three centuries of the 2nd millennium bce. The North Semitic alphabet was so constant for many centuries that it is impossible to think that there had been any material changes in the preceding two to three centuries. Moreover, the North [Semitic languages](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Semitic-languages), based as they are on a consonantal root (i.e., a system in which the vowels serve mainly to indicate grammatical or similar changes), were clearly suitable for the creation of a consonantal alphabet.

The inventor or inventors of the alphabet were, no doubt, influenced by Egyptian writing—perhaps also by other scripts. Indeed, it is probable that those who invented the alphabet were acquainted with most of the scripts current in the eastern Mediterranean lands at the time. It is now generally agreed that the originators belonged to the Northwest Semitic linguistic group, which includes the ancient Canaanites, Phoenicians, and Hebrews.

Originally, graphs were perhaps “motivated” pictorial signs that were subsequently used to represent the initial sound of the name of the pictured object. The North Semitic alphabet remained almost unaltered for many centuries. If the signs’ external form (which, it must be [emphasized](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/emphasized), had no particular significance) is ignored and only their phonetic value, number, and order are considered, the modern [Hebrew alphabet](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Hebrew-alphabet) may be regarded as a continuation of the original alphabet created more than 3,500 years ago. The Hebrew order of the letters seems to be the oldest. The earliest evidence that the Hebrew alphabet was learned systematically was left in the form of a schoolboy’s scribbling on the vertical face of the upper step of a staircase leading up to the palace at Tel Lakhish, in southern Israel. It includes the scratching of the first five letters of the early Hebrew alphabet in their [conventional](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/conventional) order, and it belongs to the 8th or 7th century bce.
