**Hydrogen** is a [chemical element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_element "Chemical element"); it has the [symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_symbol "Chemical symbol") **H** and [atomic number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_number "Atomic number") 1. It is the [lightest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_atomic_weights "List of atomic weights") and [most abundant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abundance_of_the_chemical_elements "Abundance of the chemical elements") chemical element in the universe, constituting about 75% of all [normal matter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baryon "Baryon"). Under [standard conditions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_conditions "Standard conditions"), hydrogen is a [gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gas "Gas") of [diatomic molecules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diatomic_molecule "Diatomic molecule") with the [formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_formula "Chemical formula") H2, called **dihydrogen**, or sometimes **hydrogen gas**, **molecular hydrogen**, or simply hydrogen. Dihydrogen is colorless, odorless, non-toxic, and highly [combustible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combustible "Combustible"). [Stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star "Star"), including the [Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun "Sun"), mainly consist of hydrogen in a [plasma state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plasma_state "Plasma state"), while on Earth, hydrogen is found as the gas H2 (dihydrogen) and in [molecules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molecule "Molecule"), such as in [water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water "Water") and [organic compounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organic_compound "Organic compound"). The most common [isotope of hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotope_of_hydrogen "Isotope of hydrogen"), 1H, consists of one [proton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proton "Proton"), one [electron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron "Electron"), and no [neutrons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron "Neutron").

Hydrogen gas was first produced artificially in the 17th century by the [reaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_reaction "Chemical reaction") of [acids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acid "Acid") with metals. [Henry Cavendish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Cavendish "Henry Cavendish"), in 1766–1781, identified hydrogen gas as a distinct substance and discovered its property of producing water when burned: this is the origin of hydrogen's name, which means 'water-former' (from [Ancient Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): [ὕδωρ](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/ὕδωρ#Ancient_Greek "wikt:ὕδωρ"), [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"): *húdōr*, [lit.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literal_translation "Literal translation") 'water', and [γεννάω](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/γεννάω#Ancient_Greek "wikt:γεννάω"), *gennáō*, 'I bring forth'). Understanding the [colors of light absorbed and emitted by hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_spectral_series "Hydrogen spectral series") was a crucial part of the development of [quantum mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_mechanics "Quantum mechanics").

Hydrogen, typically [nonmetallic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonmetallic "Nonmetallic") except under [extreme pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extreme_pressure "Extreme pressure"), readily forms [covalent bonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covalent_bond "Covalent bond") with most nonmetals, contributing to the formation of compounds like water and various organic substances. Its role is crucial in [acid–base reactions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acid–base_reaction "Acid–base reaction"), which mainly involve proton exchange among [soluble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solubility "Solubility") molecules. In [ionic compounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionic_compounds "Ionic compounds"), hydrogen can take the form of either a negatively-charged [anion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anion "Anion"), where it is known as [hydride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydride "Hydride"), or as a positively charged [cation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cation "Cation"), H+, [hydron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydron "Hydron"). Although tightly bonded to water molecules, hydrons strongly affect the behavior of [aqueous solutions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aqueous_solution "Aqueous solution"), as reflected in the importance of [pH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PH "PH"). Hydride, on the other hand, is rarely observed because it tends to deprotonate solvents, yielding H2.[[12]](#cite_note-12)

In the [early universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_universe "Early universe"), neutral hydrogen atoms [formed about 370,000 years after the Big Bang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Bang_nucleosynthesis "Big Bang nucleosynthesis") as the universe expanded and plasma had cooled enough for electrons to remain bound to protons. After stars [began to form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_formation "Star formation"), most of the hydrogen in the [intergalactic medium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intergalactic_medium "Intergalactic medium") was re-ionized.

Nearly all [hydrogen production](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_production "Hydrogen production") is done by transforming [fossil fuels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fossil_fuel "Fossil fuel"), particularly [steam reforming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steam_reforming "Steam reforming") of [natural gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_gas "Natural gas"). It can also be produced from water or saline by [electrolysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrolysis "Electrolysis"), but this process is more expensive. Its main industrial uses include fossil fuel processing and [ammonia production](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammonia_production "Ammonia production") for fertilizer. Emerging uses for hydrogen include the use of [fuel cells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuel_cell "Fuel cell") to generate electricity.

## Properties

### Atomic hydrogen

#### Electron energy levels

Main article: [Hydrogen atom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_atom "Hydrogen atom")

The [ground state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ground_state "Ground state") [energy level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy_level "Energy level") of the electron in a hydrogen atom is −13.6 [electronvolts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronvolts "Electronvolts") (eV),[[13]](#cite_note-13) equivalent to an [ultraviolet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultraviolet "Ultraviolet") [photon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photon "Photon") of roughly 91 [nanometers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanometer "Nanometer") wavelength.[[14]](#cite_note-14) The energy levels of hydrogen are referred to by consecutive [quantum numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_number "Quantum number"), with ![{\displaystyle n=1}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/d9ec7e1edc2e6d98f5aec2a39ae5f1c99d1e1425) being the ground state. The [hydrogen spectral series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_spectral_series "Hydrogen spectral series") corresponds to emission of light due to transitions from higher to lower energy levels.[[15]](#cite_note-15): 105 Each energy level is further split by [spin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin_(physics) "Spin (physics)") interactions between the electron and proton into four [hyperfine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperfine_structure "Hyperfine structure") levels.[[16]](#cite_note-16)

High-precision values for the hydrogen atom energy levels are required for definitions of physical constants. Quantum calculations have identified nine contributions to the energy levels. The [eigenvalue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eigenvalue "Eigenvalue") from the [Dirac equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirac_equation "Dirac equation") is the largest contribution. Other terms include [relativistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relativistic_quantum_mechanics "Relativistic quantum mechanics") recoil, the [self-energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-energy "Self-energy"), and the [vacuum polarization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vacuum_polarization "Vacuum polarization") terms.[[17]](#cite_note-17)

#### Nomenclature

The standards organization for chemical names, [IUPAC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUPAC "IUPAC"), gives general names when the context assumes natural isotope abundance or ignores the isotope. These general names are *hydrogen* for the neutral atom, *[hydron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydron "Hydron")* for the cation, H+, *[hydride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydride "Hydride")* for the anion, and H-. The name *proton* is often used for the positively charged cation, but this is strictly correct only for the cation of the dominant isotope 1  
H.[[18]](#cite_note-iupac1988proton-18)

#### Isotopes

Main article: [Isotopes of hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotopes_of_hydrogen "Isotopes of hydrogen")

[![Diagram showing the structure of each of Hydrogen-1 (mass number 1, 1 electron, 1 proton), Hydrogen-2 or deuterium (mass number 2, 1 electron, 1 proton, 1 neutron), and Hydrogen-3 or tritium (mass number 3, 1 electron, 1 proton, 2 neutrons)](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1c/Blausen_0530_HydrogenIsotopes.png/250px-Blausen_0530_HydrogenIsotopes.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Blausen_0530_HydrogenIsotopes.png)

The three naturally-occurring isotopes of hydrogen: hydrogen-1 (protium), hydrogen-2 (deuterium), and hydrogen-3 (tritium)

Hydrogen has three naturally-occurring isotopes, denoted 1  
H, 2  
H and 3  
H. Other, highly-unstable [nuclides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclide "Nuclide") (4  
H to 7  
H) have been [synthesized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nucleosynthesis "Nucleosynthesis") in laboratories but not observed in nature.[[19]](#cite_note-Gurov-19)[[20]](#cite_note-Korsheninnikov-20)

**1  
H** is the most common hydrogen isotope, with an abundance of >99.98%. Because the [nucleus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_nucleus "Atomic nucleus") of this isotope consists of only a single proton, it is given the descriptive but rarely used formal name *protium*.[[21]](#cite_note-21) It is the only stable isotope with no neutrons (see [diproton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diproton "Diproton") for a discussion of why others do not exist).[[11]](#cite_note-NUBASE2020-11)

**2  
H**, the other stable hydrogen isotope, is known as [deuterium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deuterium "Deuterium") and contains one proton and one [neutron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron "Neutron") in the nucleus. Nearly all deuterium nuclei in the universe are thought to have been produced in [Big Bang nucleosynthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Bang_nucleosynthesis "Big Bang nucleosynthesis"), and have endured since then.[[22]](#cite_note-22): 24.2 Deuterium is not radioactive, and is not a significant toxicity hazard. Water enriched in molecules that include deuterium instead of normal hydrogen is called [heavy water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_water "Heavy water"). Deuterium and its compounds are used as a non-radioactive label in chemical experiments and in solvents for 1  
H-[NMR spectroscopy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NMR_spectroscopy "NMR spectroscopy").[[23]](#cite_note-23) Heavy water is used as a [neutron moderator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_moderator "Neutron moderator") and coolant for nuclear reactors. Deuterium is also a potential fuel for commercial [nuclear fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_fusion "Nuclear fusion").[[24]](#cite_note-24)

**3  
H** is known as [tritium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tritium "Tritium") and contains one proton and two neutrons in its nucleus. It is radioactive, decaying into [helium-3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helium-3 "Helium-3") through [beta decay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_decay "Beta decay") with a [half-life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half-life "Half-life") of 12.32 years.[[25]](#cite_note-Miessler-25) It is radioactive enough to be used in [luminous paint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radioluminescent_paint "Radioluminescent paint") to enhance the visibility of data displays, such as for painting the hands and dial-markers of watches. The watch glass prevents the small amount of radiation from escaping the case.[[26]](#cite_note-Traub95-26) Small amounts of tritium are produced naturally by [cosmic rays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_rays "Cosmic rays") striking atmospheric gases; tritium has also been released in [nuclear weapons tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapons_tests "Nuclear weapons tests").[[27]](#cite_note-27) It is used in nuclear fusion,[[28]](#cite_note-28) as a tracer in [isotope geochemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotope_geochemistry "Isotope geochemistry"),[[29]](#cite_note-29) and in specialized [self-powered lighting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-powered_lighting "Self-powered lighting") devices.[[30]](#cite_note-30) Tritium has also been used in chemical and biological labeling experiments as a [radiolabel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiolabel "Radiolabel").[[31]](#cite_note-holte-31)

Unique among the elements, distinct names are assigned to hydrogen's isotopes in common use. During the early study of radioactivity, heavy radioisotopes were given their own names, but these are mostly no longer used. The symbols D and T (instead of 2  
H and 3  
H) are sometimes used for deuterium and tritium, but the symbol P was already used for [phosphorus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosphorus "Phosphorus") and thus was not available for protium.[[32]](#cite_note-32) In its [nomenclatural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUPAC_nomenclature "IUPAC nomenclature") guidelines, the [International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Union_of_Pure_and_Applied_Chemistry "International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry") (IUPAC) allows any of D, T, 2  
H, and 3  
H to be used, though 2  
H and 3  
H are preferred.[[33]](#cite_note-33)

[Antihydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antihydrogen "Antihydrogen") (H) is the [antimatter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antimatter "Antimatter") counterpart to hydrogen. It consists of an [anti­proton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiproton "Antiproton") with a [positron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Positron "Positron").[[34]](#cite_note-char15-34)[[35]](#cite_note-Keller15-35) The [exotic atom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exotic_atom "Exotic atom") [muonium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muonium "Muonium") (symbol Mu), composed of an [antimuon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antimuon "Antimuon") and an [electron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron "Electron"), is the anti­matter analogue of hydrogen; IUPAC nomenclature incorporates such hypothetical compounds as muonium chloride (MuCl) and sodium muonide (NaMu), analogous to [hydrogen chloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_chloride "Hydrogen chloride") and [sodium hydride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_hydride "Sodium hydride") respectively.[[36]](#cite_note-iupac-36)

### Dihydrogen

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bb/Dihydrogen-3D-balls.png/250px-Dihydrogen-3D-balls.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dihydrogen-3D-balls.png)

The structure of dihydrogen

Under [standard conditions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_conditions "Standard conditions"), hydrogen is a [gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gas "Gas") of [diatomic molecules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diatomic_molecule "Diatomic molecule") with the [formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_formula "Chemical formula") H2, officially called "dihydrogen",[[37]](#cite_note-37): 308 but also called "molecular hydrogen",[[38]](#cite_note-britannica-38) or simply hydrogen. Dihydrogen is a colorless, odorless, flammable gas.[[38]](#cite_note-britannica-38)

#### Combustion

Combustion of hydrogen with the oxygen in the air. When the bottom cap is removed, allowing air to enter, hydrogen in the container rises and burns as it mixes with the air.

Hydrogen gas is highly flammable, reacting with [oxygen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen "Oxygen") in air to produce liquid water:

2 H2(g) + O2(g) → 2 H2O(l)

The [amount of heat released](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enthalpy_of_combustion "Enthalpy of combustion") per [mole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mole_(unit) "Mole (unit)") of hydrogen is −286 [kilojoules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilojoules "Kilojoules") (kJ), or 141.9 [megajoules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megajoules "Megajoules") (MJ) for a one-kilogram (2.2 lb) mass (based on the [higher heating value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher_heating_value "Higher heating value") measurement).[[39]](#cite_note-39)

Hydrogen gas forms explosive mixtures with air in concentrations from 4%–74%[[40]](#cite_note-40) and with chlorine at 5%–95%. The hydrogen [autoignition temperature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autoignition_temperature "Autoignition temperature"), the temperature of spontaneous ignition in air, is 500 °C (932 °F).[[41]](#cite_note-41) In a high-pressure [hydrogen leak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_leak "Hydrogen leak"), the shock wave from the leak itself can heat air to the autoignition temperature, leading to flaming and possibly explosion.[[42]](#cite_note-42)

Hydrogen flames emit faint blue and [ultraviolet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultraviolet "Ultraviolet") light.[[43]](#cite_note-43) [Flame detectors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flame_detector "Flame detector") are used to detect hydrogen fires as they are nearly invisible to the naked eye in daylight.[[44]](#cite_note-44)[[45]](#cite_note-spinoff-2016-45)

#### Spin isomers

Main article: [Spin isomers of hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin_isomers_of_hydrogen "Spin isomers of hydrogen")

Molecular H2 exists as two [nuclear isomers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_isomer "Nuclear isomer") that differ in the [spin states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin_(physics) "Spin (physics)") of their nuclei.[[46]](#cite_note-uigi-46) In the **ortho­hydrogen** form, the spins of the two nuclei are parallel, forming a spin [triplet state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triplet_state "Triplet state") having a [total molecular spin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_molecular_spin "Total molecular spin") ![{\displaystyle S=1}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/d5e2b58c1aaaf2718fb801e97bf21d1f72726372); in the **para­hydrogen** form the spins are anti­parallel and form a spin [singlet state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singlet_state "Singlet state") having spin ![{\displaystyle S=0}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/4ae0fc3192b864f55a46749d8a64e7cf7783d04c). The equilibrium ratio of ortho- to para-hydrogen depends on temperature. At room temperature or warmer, equilibrium hydrogen gas contains about 25% of the para form and 75% of the ortho form.[[47]](#cite_note-Green2012-47) The ortho form is an [excited state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excited_state "Excited state"), having higher energy than the para form by 1.455 [kJ/mol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joule_per_mole "Joule per mole"),[[48]](#cite_note-PlanckInstitut-48) and it converts to the para form over the course of several minutes when cooled to low temperature.[[49]](#cite_note-49) The thermal properties of these isomers differ because each has distinct [rotational quantum states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotational–vibrational_spectroscopy "Rotational–vibrational spectroscopy").[[50]](#cite_note-NASA-50)

The ortho-to-para ratio in H2 is an important consideration in the [liquefaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquefaction "Liquefaction") and storage of [liquid hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_hydrogen "Liquid hydrogen"): the conversion from ortho to para is [exothermic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exothermic "Exothermic"), and produces sufficient heat to evaporate most of the liquid if the conversion to para­hydrogen does not occur during the cooling process.[[51]](#cite_note-Amos98-51) [Catalysts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalyst "Catalyst") for the ortho-para inter­conversion, such as [ferric oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferric_oxide "Ferric oxide") and [activated carbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Activated_carbon "Activated carbon") compounds, are therefore used during hydrogen cooling to avoid this loss of liquid.[[52]](#cite_note-Svadlenak-52)

#### Phases

[![Phase diagram of hydrogen on logarithmic scales. Lines show boundaries between phases, with the end of the liquid-gas line indicating the critical point. The triple point of hydrogen is just off-scale to the left.](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/31/Phase_diagram_of_hydrogen.png/250px-Phase_diagram_of_hydrogen.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Phase_diagram_of_hydrogen.png)

[Phase diagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phase_diagram "Phase diagram") of hydrogen with a [logarithmic scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logarithmic_scale "Logarithmic scale"). The left edge corresponds to about one [atmosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmosphere_(unit) "Atmosphere (unit)").[[53]](#cite_note-53)

[Liquid hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_hydrogen "Liquid hydrogen") can exist at temperatures below hydrogen's [critical point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critical_point_(thermodynamics) "Critical point (thermodynamics)") of 33 [kelvins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelvin "Kelvin") (−240.2 °C; −400.3 °F).[[54]](#cite_note-54) However, for it to be in a fully liquid state at [atmospheric pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_pressure "Atmospheric pressure"), H2 needs to be cooled to 20.28 K (−252.87 °C; −423.17 °F). Hydrogen was liquefied by [James Dewar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Dewar "James Dewar") in 1898 by using [regenerative cooling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regenerative_cooling "Regenerative cooling") and his invention, the [vacuum flask](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vacuum_flask "Vacuum flask").[[55]](#cite_note-55)

Liquid hydrogen becomes [solid hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid_hydrogen "Solid hydrogen") at [standard pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_pressure "Standard pressure") below hydrogen's [melting point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melting_point "Melting point") of 14.01 K (−259.14 °C; −434.45 °F). Distinct solid phases exist, known as Phase I through Phase V, each exhibiting a characteristic molecular arrangement.[[56]](#cite_note-Helled2020-56) Liquid and solid phases can exist in combination at the [triple point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple_point "Triple point"); this mixture is known as [slush hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slush_hydrogen "Slush hydrogen").[[57]](#cite_note-57)

[Metallic hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallic_hydrogen "Metallic hydrogen"), a phase obtained at extremely high pressures (in excess of 400 [billion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1000000000_(number) "1000000000 (number)") [Pa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pascal_(unit) "Pascal (unit)") (58,000,000 [psi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pound_per_square_inch "Pound per square inch"))), is an electrical conductor. It is believed to exist deep within [giant planets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant_planet "Giant planet") like [Jupiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jupiter "Jupiter").[[56]](#cite_note-Helled2020-56)[[58]](#cite_note-58)

When [ionized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionized "Ionized"), hydrogen becomes a [plasma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plasma_(physics) "Plasma (physics)"). This is the form in which hydrogen exists within [stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star "Star").[[59]](#cite_note-59)
