## History

For a chronological guide, see [Timeline of hydrogen technologies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_hydrogen_technologies "Timeline of hydrogen technologies").

### 17th century

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/61/Portret_van_Robert_Boyle%2C_RP-P-OB-4578_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Portret_van_Robert_Boyle%2C_RP-P-OB-4578_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Portret_van_Robert_Boyle,_RP-P-OB-4578_(cropped).jpg)

[Robert Boyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Boyle "Robert Boyle"), who discovered the reaction between [iron filings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_filings "Iron filings") and dilute acids

In 1671, Irish scientist [Robert Boyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Boyle "Robert Boyle") discovered and described the reaction between [iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron "Iron") filings and dilute [acids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acid "Acid"), which results in the production of hydrogen gas.[[62]](#cite_note-62)[[63]](#cite_note-63) Boyle did not note that the gas was flammable, but hydrogen would play a key role in overturning the [phlogiston theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phlogiston_theory "Phlogiston theory") of combustion.[[64]](#cite_note-Ramsay-1896-64)

### 18th century

In 1766, [Henry Cavendish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Cavendish "Henry Cavendish") was the first to recognize hydrogen gas as a discrete substance, by naming the gas from a [metal-acid reaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metal-acid_reaction "Metal-acid reaction") "inflammable air". He speculated that "inflammable air" was in fact identical to the hypothetical substance "[phlogiston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phlogiston_theory "Phlogiston theory")"[[65]](#cite_note-65)[[66]](#cite_note-cav766-66) and further finding in 1781 that the gas produces water when burned. He is usually given credit for the discovery of hydrogen as an element.[[9]](#cite_note-Nostrand-9)[[8]](#cite_note-nbb-8)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/00/Antoine-Laurent_Lavoisier_by_Louis_Jean_Desire_Delaistre_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Antoine-Laurent_Lavoisier_by_Louis_Jean_Desire_Delaistre_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Antoine-Laurent_Lavoisier_by_Louis_Jean_Desire_Delaistre_(cropped).jpg)

[Antoine Lavoisier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoine_Lavoisier "Antoine Lavoisier"), who identified the element that came to be known as hydrogen

In 1783, [Antoine Lavoisier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoine_Lavoisier "Antoine Lavoisier") identified the element that came to be known as hydrogen[[67]](#cite_note-67) when he and [Laplace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre-Simon_Laplace "Pierre-Simon Laplace") reproduced Cavendish's finding that water is produced when hydrogen is burned.[[8]](#cite_note-nbb-8) Lavoisier produced hydrogen for his experiments on [mass conservation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_conservation "Mass conservation") by treating metallic [iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron "Iron") with a stream of water through an incandescent iron tube heated in a fire. Anaerobic [oxidation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxidation "Oxidation") of iron by the protons of water at high temperature can be schematically represented by the set of following reactions:

* Fe + H2O → FeO + H2
* 2 Fe + 3 H2O → Fe2O3 + 3 H2
* 3 Fe + 4 H2O → Fe3O4 + 4 H2

Many metals react similarly with water, leading to the production of hydrogen.[[68]](#cite_note-68) In some situations, this H2-producing process is problematic, for instance in the case of [zirconium cladding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zirconium_cladding?action=edit&redlink=1 "Zirconium cladding (page does not exist)") on [nuclear fuel rods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_fuel_rod "Nuclear fuel rod").[[69]](#cite_note-69)

### 19th century

By 1806 hydrogen was used to fill [balloons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balloon "Balloon").[[70]](#cite_note-70) [François Isaac de Rivaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/François_Isaac_de_Rivaz "François Isaac de Rivaz") built the first [de Rivaz engine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Rivaz_engine "De Rivaz engine"), an internal combustion engine powered by a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen, in 1806. [Edward Daniel Clarke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Daniel_Clarke "Edward Daniel Clarke") invented the hydrogen gas blowpipe in 1819. The [Döbereiner's lamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Döbereiner's_lamp "Döbereiner's lamp") and [limelight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limelight "Limelight") were invented in 1823. Hydrogen was [liquefied](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_hydrogen "Liquid hydrogen") for the first time by [James Dewar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Dewar "James Dewar") in 1898 by using [regenerative cooling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regenerative_cooling "Regenerative cooling") and his invention, the [vacuum flask](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vacuum_flask "Vacuum flask"). He produced [solid hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid_hydrogen "Solid hydrogen") the next year.[[8]](#cite_note-nbb-8)

One of the first [quantum effects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_effects "Quantum effects") to be explicitly noticed, although not understood at the time, was [James Clerk Maxwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Clerk_Maxwell "James Clerk Maxwell")'s observation that the [specific heat capacity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Specific_heat_capacity "Specific heat capacity") of H2 unaccountably departs from that of a [diatomic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diatomic "Diatomic") gas below room temperature, and begins to increasingly resemble that of a monatomic gas at cryogenic temperatures. According to quantum theory, this behavior arises from the spacing of the ([quantized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantization_(physics) "Quantization (physics)")) [rotational energy levels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotational_energy_levels?action=edit&redlink=1 "Rotational energy levels (page does not exist)"), which are particularly wide-spaced in H2 because of its low mass. These widely-spaced levels inhibit equal partition of heat energy into rotational motion in hydrogen at low temperatures. Diatomic gases composed of heavier atoms do not have such widely spaced levels and do not exhibit the same effect.[[71]](#cite_note-Berman-71)

### 20th century

The existence of the [hydride anion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydride_anion "Hydride anion") was suggested by [Gilbert N. Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilbert_N._Lewis "Gilbert N. Lewis") in 1916 for [group 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_1_elements "Group 1 elements") and [group 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_2_elements "Group 2 elements") salt-like compounds. In 1920, Moers electrolyzed molten [lithium hydride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithium_hydride "Lithium hydride") (LiH), producing a [stoichiometric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoichiometric "Stoichiometric") quantity of hydrogen at the [anode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anode "Anode").[[72]](#cite_note-Moers-72)

[![A line spectrum showing black background with narrow lines superimposed on it: one violet, one blue, one cyan, and one red.](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/Emission_spectrum-H_labeled.svg/250px-Emission_spectrum-H_labeled.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Emission_spectrum-H_labeled.svg)

Hydrogen emission spectrum lines in the four visible lines of the [Balmer series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balmer_series "Balmer series")

Because of its simple atomic structure, consisting only of a proton and an electron, the [hydrogen atom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_atom "Hydrogen atom"), together with the [spectrum of light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_spectral_series "Hydrogen spectral series") produced from it or absorbed by it, has been central to the [development of the theory of atomic structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_atomic_theory "History of atomic theory").[[73]](#cite_note-73) The energy levels of hydrogen can be calculated fairly accurately using the [Bohr model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohr_model "Bohr model") of the atom, in which the electron "orbits" the proton, just as Earth orbits the Sun. However, the electron and proton are held together by [electrostatic attraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrostatic_attraction "Electrostatic attraction"), while planets and celestial objects are held by [gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravity "Gravity"). Due to the [discretization](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/discretization "wikt:discretization") of [angular momentum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angular_momentum "Angular momentum") postulated in early [quantum mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_mechanics "Quantum mechanics") by Bohr, the electron in the Bohr model can only occupy certain allowed distances from the proton, and therefore only certain allowed energies.[[74]](#cite_note-74)

Hydrogen's unique position as the only neutral atom for which the [Schrödinger equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schrödinger_equation "Schrödinger equation") can be directly solved has significantly contributed to the understanding of quantum mechanics through the exploration of its energetics.[[75]](#cite_note-Laursen04-75) Furthermore, study of the corresponding simplicity of the hydrogen molecule and the corresponding [cation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cation "Cation"), [H+2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H2+ "H2+"), brought understanding of the nature of the [chemical bond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_bond "Chemical bond"), which followed shortly after the quantum mechanical treatment of the hydrogen atom had been developed in the mid-1920s.[[76]](#cite_note-76)

#### Hydrogen-lifted airship

[![Airship Hindenburg over New York](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/59/Hindenburg_over_New_York_1937_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Hindenburg_over_New_York_1937_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hindenburg_over_New_York_1937_(cropped).jpg)

The [*Hindenburg*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindenburg-class_airship "Hindenburg-class airship") over [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") in 1937

Because H2 has only 7% the density of air, it was once widely used as a [lifting gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lifting_gas "Lifting gas") in balloons and [airships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airship "Airship").[[77]](#cite_note-Almqvist03-77) The first hydrogen-filled balloon was invented by [Jacques Charles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Charles "Jacques Charles") in 1783. Hydrogen provided the lift for the first reliable form of air-travel following the 1852 invention of the first hydrogen-lifted airship by [Henri Giffard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Giffard "Henri Giffard"). German count [Ferdinand von Zeppelin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_von_Zeppelin "Ferdinand von Zeppelin") promoted the idea of rigid airships lifted by hydrogen that later were called [Zeppelins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeppelin "Zeppelin"), the first of which had its maiden flight in 1900.[[8]](#cite_note-nbb-8) Regularly-scheduled flights started in 1910 and by the outbreak of World War I in August 1914, they had carried 35,000 passengers without a serious incident. Hydrogen-lifted airships in the form of [blimps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blimp "Blimp") were used as observation platforms and bombers during World War II, especially on the [US Eastern seaboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Eastern_seaboard "US Eastern seaboard").[[78]](#cite_note-78)

The first non-stop transatlantic crossing was made by the British airship *[R34](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R34_(airship) "R34 (airship)")* in 1919 and regular passenger service resumed in the 1920s. Hydrogen was used in the [*Hindenburg*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LZ_129_Hindenburg "LZ 129 Hindenburg"), which caught fire over [New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey "New Jersey") on 6 May 1937.[[8]](#cite_note-nbb-8) The hydrogen that filled the airship was ignited, possibly by static electricity, and burst into flames.[[79]](#cite_note-79) Following this [disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindenburg_disaster "Hindenburg disaster"), commercial hydrogen airship travel [ceased](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rigid_airship#Demise "Rigid airship"). Hydrogen is still used, in preference to non-flammable but more expensive [helium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helium "Helium"), as a lifting gas for [weather balloons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_balloon#Materials_and_equipment "Weather balloon").[[80]](#cite_note-80)

#### Deuterium and tritium

[Deuterium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deuterium "Deuterium") was discovered in December 1931 by [Harold Urey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Urey "Harold Urey"), and [tritium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tritium "Tritium") was prepared in 1934 by [Ernest Rutherford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_Rutherford "Ernest Rutherford"), [Mark Oliphant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Oliphant "Mark Oliphant"), and [Paul Harteck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Harteck "Paul Harteck").[[9]](#cite_note-Nostrand-9) [Heavy water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_water "Heavy water"), which consists of deuterium in the place of regular hydrogen, was discovered by Urey's group in 1932.[[8]](#cite_note-nbb-8)

## Chemistry

### Reactions of H2

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/84/HFe_H2_dppe_2.svg/250px-HFe_H2_dppe_2.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:HFe_H2_dppe_2.svg)

A [dihydrogen complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dihydrogen_complex "Dihydrogen complex") of iron, [HFe(H2)(dppe)2]+

H2 is relatively unreactive. The thermodynamic basis of this low reactivity is the very strong H–H bond, with a [bond dissociation energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bond_dissociation_energy "Bond dissociation energy") of 435.7 [kJ/mol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joule_per_mole "Joule per mole").[[81]](#cite_note-81) It does form coordination complexes called [dihydrogen complexes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dihydrogen_complex "Dihydrogen complex"). These species provide insights into the early steps in the interactions of hydrogen with metal catalysts. According to [neutron diffraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_diffraction "Neutron diffraction"), the metal and two H atoms form a triangle in these complexes. The H-H bond remains intact but is elongated. They are acidic.[[82]](#cite_note-82)

Although exotic on Earth, the H+3 ion is common in the universe. It is a triangular species, like the aforementioned dihydrogen complexes. It is known as [protonated molecular hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trihydrogen_cation "Trihydrogen cation") or the trihydrogen cation.[[83]](#cite_note-Carrington-83)

Hydrogen reacts with [chlorine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chlorine "Chlorine") to produce [HCl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HCl "HCl"), and with [bromine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bromine "Bromine") to produce [HBr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_bromide "Hydrogen bromide"), via a [chain reaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chain_reaction "Chain reaction"). The reaction requires initiation. For example, in the case of Br2, the dibromine molecule is split apart: Br2 + (UV light) → 2Br•. Propagating reactions consume hydrogen molecules and produce HBr, as well as Br and H atoms:

Br• + H2 → HBr + H

H + Br2 → HBr +Br

Finally the terminating reaction:

H + HBr → H2 + Br•

2 Br• → Br2

consumes the remaining atoms.[[84]](#cite_note-84): 289

The addition of H2 to [unsaturated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturated_and_unsaturated_compounds "Saturated and unsaturated compounds") organic compounds, such as [alkenes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkene "Alkene") and [alkynes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkyne "Alkyne"), is called [hydrogenation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogenation "Hydrogenation"). Even if the reaction is [energetically favorable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exothermic "Exothermic"), it does not occur spontaneously even at higher temperatures. In the presence of a [catalyst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalyst "Catalyst") like finely divided [platinum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platinum "Platinum") or [nickel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nickel "Nickel"), the reaction proceeds at room temperature.[[85]](#cite_note-85): 477

### Hydrogen-containing compounds

Main article: [Hydrogen compounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_compounds "Hydrogen compounds")

Hydrogen can exist in both +1 and −1 [oxidation states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxidation_state "Oxidation state"), forming compounds through [ionic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionic_bonding "Ionic bonding") and [covalent bonding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covalent_bonding "Covalent bonding"). The element is part of a wide range of substances, including water, [hydrocarbons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrocarbon "Hydrocarbon"), and numerous other [organic compounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organic_compound "Organic compound").[[86]](#cite_note-hydrocarbon-86) The H+ ion—commonly referred to as a proton due to its single proton and absence of electrons—is central to [acid–base chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acid–base_reaction "Acid–base reaction"), although the proton does not move freely. In the [Brønsted–Lowry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brønsted–Lowry_acids "Brønsted–Lowry acids") framework, acids are defined by their ability to donate H+ ions to bases.[[87]](#cite_note-87)

Hydrogen forms a vast variety of compounds with [carbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon "Carbon"), known as hydrocarbons, and an even greater diversity with other elements ([heteroatoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heteroatom "Heteroatom")), giving rise to the broad class of organic compounds often associated with living organisms.[[86]](#cite_note-hydrocarbon-86)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7a/NaH.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:NaH.jpg)

A sample of [sodium hydride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_hydride "Sodium hydride")

Hydrogen compounds with hydrogen in the oxidation state −1 are known as [hydrides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydride "Hydride"), which are usually formed between hydrogen and metals. The hydrides can be ionic (aka saline), covalent, or metallic. With heating, H2 reacts efficiently with the [alkali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkali_earth_metals "Alkali earth metals") and [alkaline earth metals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkaline_earth_metal "Alkaline earth metal") to give the [ionic hydrides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionic_hydrides "Ionic hydrides") of the formulas MH and MH2, respectively. These salt-like crystalline compounds have high melting points and all react with water to liberate hydrogen. Covalent hydrides include [boranes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borane "Borane") and polymeric [aluminium hydride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium_hydride "Aluminium hydride"). [Transition metals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transition_metal "Transition metal") form [metal hydrides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metal_hydride "Metal hydride") via continuous dissolution of hydrogen into the metal.[[88]](#cite_note-UllmannH2-88) A well-known hydride is [lithium aluminium hydride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithium_aluminium_hydride "Lithium aluminium hydride"): the [AlH4]− anion carries hydridic centers firmly attached to the Al(III).[[89]](#cite_note-89) Perhaps the most extensive series of hydrides are the [boranes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borane "Borane"), compounds consisting only of boron and hydrogen.[[90]](#cite_note-Downs-90)

Hydrides can bond to these [electropositive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electropositive "Electropositive") elements not only as a terminal [ligand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ligand "Ligand") but also as [bridging ligands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridging_ligand "Bridging ligand"). In diborane (B2H6), four hydrogen atoms are terminal, while two bridge between the two boron atoms.[[25]](#cite_note-Miessler-25)

### Hydrogen bonding

Main article: [Hydrogen bond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_bond "Hydrogen bond")

When bonded to a more [electronegative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronegative "Electronegative") element, particularly [fluorine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluorine "Fluorine"), [oxygen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen "Oxygen"), or [nitrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen "Nitrogen"), hydrogen can participate in a form of medium-strength noncovalent bonding with another electronegative element with a [lone pair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lone_pair "Lone pair") like oxygen or nitrogen. This phenomenon, called [hydrogen bonding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_bonding "Hydrogen bonding"), is critical to the stability of many biological molecules.[[91]](#cite_note-91): 375[[92]](#cite_note-92) Hydrogen bonding alters molecule structures, [viscosity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viscosity "Viscosity"), [solubility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solubility "Solubility"), melting and boiling points, and even [protein folding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protein_folding "Protein folding") dynamics.[[93]](#cite_note-93)

### Protons and acids

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/Base_pair_AT.svg/250px-Base_pair_AT.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Base_pair_AT.svg)

An "A-T [base pair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Base_pair "Base pair")" in DNA illustrating how hydrogen bonds are critical to the [genetic code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetic_code "Genetic code"). The drawing illustrates that in many chemical depictions, C-H bonds are not always shown explicitly, an indication of their pervasiveness.

In water, hydrogen bonding plays an important role in reaction thermodynamics. A hydrogen bond can shift over to proton transfer. Under the [Brønsted–Lowry acid–base theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brønsted–Lowry_acid–base_theory "Brønsted–Lowry acid–base theory"), acids are proton donors, while bases are proton acceptors.[[94]](#cite_note-94): 28 A bare proton (H+) essentially cannot exist in anything other than a vacuum. Otherwise it attaches to other atoms, ions, or molecules. Even chemical species as inert as [methane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methane "Methane") can be protonated. The term "proton" is used loosely and metaphorically to refer to solvated hydrogen [cations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cation "Cation") attached to other chemical species; it is denoted "H+" without any implication that any single protons exist freely in solution as a species. To avoid the implication of the naked proton in solution, acidic aqueous solutions are sometimes considered to contain the "[hydronium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydronium "Hydronium") ion" ([H3O]+), or still more accurately, [H9O4]+.[[95]](#cite_note-Okumura-95) Other [oxonium ions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxonium_ion "Oxonium ion") are found when water is in acidic solution with other solvents.[[96]](#cite_note-Perdoncin-96)

The concentration of these solvated protons determines the [pH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PH "PH") of a solution, a [logarithmic scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logarithmic_scale "Logarithmic scale") that reflects its acidity or basicity. Lower pH values indicate higher concentrations of hydronium ions, corresponding to more acidic conditions.[[97]](#cite_note-housecroft-97)

## Occurrence

### Cosmic

[![A white-green cotton-like clog on black background.](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7a/Nursery_of_New_Stars_-_GPN-2000-000972.jpg/250px-Nursery_of_New_Stars_-_GPN-2000-000972.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nursery_of_New_Stars_-_GPN-2000-000972.jpg)

[NGC 604](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NGC_604 "NGC 604"), a giant [region of ionized hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H_II_region "H II region") in the [Triangulum Galaxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangulum_Galaxy "Triangulum Galaxy")

Hydrogen, as atomic H, is the most [abundant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_abundance "Natural abundance") [chemical element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_element "Chemical element") in the universe, making up 75% of [normal matter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baryon "Baryon") by [mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass "Mass").[[98]](#cite_note-98) and >90% by number of atoms.[[99]](#cite_note-99) In the [early universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_universe "Early universe"), protons [formed in the first second after the Big Bang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Bang_baryogenesis "Big Bang baryogenesis"); neutral hydrogen atoms formed about 370,000 years later during the [recombination epoch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recombination_(cosmology) "Recombination (cosmology)") as the universe expanded and plasma had cooled enough for electrons to remain bound to protons.[[100]](#cite_note-100)

In astrophysics, neutral hydrogen in the [interstellar medium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstellar_medium "Interstellar medium") is called *H I* and ionized hydrogen is called *H II*.[[101]](#cite_note-101) Radiation from stars ionizes H I to H II, creating [spheres of ionized H II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strömgren_sphere "Strömgren sphere") around stars. In the [chronology of the universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chronology_of_the_universe "Chronology of the universe") neutral hydrogen dominated until the birth of stars during the era of [reionization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reionization "Reionization"), which then produced bubbles of ionized hydrogen that grew and merged over hundreds of millions of years.[[102]](#cite_note-102) These are the source of the 21-centimeter [hydrogen line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_line "Hydrogen line"), at 1420 [MHz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megahertz "Megahertz"), that is detected in order to probe primordial hydrogen. The large amount of neutral hydrogen found in the [damped Lyman-alpha systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damped_Lyman-alpha_system "Damped Lyman-alpha system") is thought to dominate the [cosmological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_cosmology "Physical cosmology") [baryonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baryon "Baryon") density of the universe up to a [redshift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redshift "Redshift") of *z* = 4.[[103]](#cite_note-103)

Hydrogen is found in great abundance in stars and [gas giant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gas_giant "Gas giant") planets. [Molecular clouds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molecular_cloud "Molecular cloud") of H2 are associated with [star formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_formation "Star formation"). Hydrogen plays a vital role in powering [stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star "Star") through the [proton-proton reaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proton-proton_reaction "Proton-proton reaction") in lower-mass stars, and through the [CNO cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNO_cycle "CNO cycle") of [nuclear fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_fusion "Nuclear fusion") in stars more massive than the [Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun "Sun").[[104]](#cite_note-104)

[Protonated molecular hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protonated_molecular_hydrogen "Protonated molecular hydrogen") (H+3) is found in the [interstellar medium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstellar_medium "Interstellar medium"), where it is generated by ionization of molecular hydrogen by [cosmic rays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_ray "Cosmic ray"). This ion has also been observed in the [upper atmosphere of Jupiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primary_atmosphere "Primary atmosphere"). The ion is long-lived in outer space due to the low temperature and density. H+3 is one of the most abundant ions in the universe, and it plays a notable role in the chemistry of the interstellar medium.[[105]](#cite_note-105) Neutral [triatomic hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triatomic_hydrogen "Triatomic hydrogen") H3 can exist only in an excited form and is unstable.[[106]](#cite_note-couple-106)

### Terrestrial

Hydrogen is the third most abundant element on the Earth's surface,[[107]](#cite_note-ArgonneBasic-107) mostly existing within [chemical compounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_compound "Chemical compound") such as [hydrocarbons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrocarbon "Hydrocarbon") and water.[[25]](#cite_note-Miessler-25) Elemental hydrogen is normally in the form of a gas, H2, at [standard conditions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_conditions "Standard conditions"). It is present in a very low concentration in Earth's atmosphere (around 0.53 [parts per million](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parts_per_million "Parts per million") on a [molar basis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mole_(unit) "Mole (unit)")[[108]](#cite_note-Grinter-108)) because of its light weight, which enables it to [escape the atmosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_escape "Atmospheric escape") more rapidly than heavier gases. Despite its low concentration in the atmosphere, terrestrial hydrogen is sufficiently abundant to support the metabolism of several varieties of bacteria.[[109]](#cite_note-109)

Large underground deposits of hydrogen gas have been discovered in several countries including [Mali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mali "Mali"), [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France") and [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia").[[110]](#cite_note-Pearce-2024-110) As of 2024, it is uncertain how much underground hydrogen can be extracted economically.[[110]](#cite_note-Pearce-2024-110)

## Production and storage

Main article: [Hydrogen production](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_production "Hydrogen production")

### Industrial routes

Nearly all of the world's current supply of hydrogen gas (H2) is produced from fossil fuels,[[111]](#cite_note-111)[[112]](#cite_note-rosenow-2022-112): 1 with less than 1% of hydrogen being produced by low-emissions technologies in 2025.[[113]](#cite_note-113) Many methods exist for producing H2, but three dominate commercially: steam reforming often coupled to water-gas shift, partial oxidation of hydrocarbons, and water electrolysis.[[114]](#cite_note-KO-114)

#### Steam reforming

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/eb/SMR%2BWGS-1.png/250px-SMR%2BWGS-1.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SMR+WGS-1.png)

Inputs and outputs of steam reforming (SMR) and water gas shift (WGS) reaction of natural gas, a process used in hydrogen production

Hydrogen is mainly produced by [steam methane reforming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steam_methane_reforming "Steam methane reforming") (SMR), the reaction of water and methane.[[115]](#cite_note-rotech-115)[[116]](#cite_note-Oxtoby-116) Thus, at high temperature (1,000–1,400 K [730–1,130 °C; 1,340–2,060 °F]), [steam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steam "Steam") (water vapor) reacts with [methane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methane "Methane") to yield [carbon monoxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_monoxide "Carbon monoxide") and H2.

CH4 + H2O → CO + 3 H2

Producing one [tonne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonne "Tonne") of hydrogen through this process emits 6.6–9.3 tonnes of carbon dioxide.[[117]](#cite_note-Bonheure-2021-117) The production of natural gas feedstock also produces emissions such as [vented](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gas_venting "Gas venting") and [fugitive methane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fugitive_gas_emissions "Fugitive gas emissions"), which further contributes to the overall carbon footprint of hydrogen.[[118]](#cite_note-Griffiths-20212-118)

This reaction is favored at low pressures but is nonetheless conducted at high pressures (2.0 [MPa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pascal_(unit) "Pascal (unit)") [20 [atm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmosphere_(unit) "Atmosphere (unit)"); 590 [inHg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inch_of_mercury "Inch of mercury")]) because high-pressure H2 is the most marketable product, and [pressure swing adsorption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pressure_swing_adsorption "Pressure swing adsorption") (PSA) purification systems work better at higher pressures. The product mixture is known as "[synthesis gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthesis_gas "Synthesis gas")" because it is often used directly for the production of [methanol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methanol "Methanol") and many other compounds. [Hydrocarbons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrocarbon "Hydrocarbon") other than methane can be used to produce synthesis gas with varying product ratios. One of the many complications to this highly-optimized technology is the formation of [coke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coke_(fuel) "Coke (fuel)") or carbon:

CH4 → C + 2 H2

Therefore, steam reforming typically employs an excess of H2O. Additional hydrogen can be recovered from the steam by using carbon monoxide through the [water gas shift reaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_gas_shift_reaction "Water gas shift reaction") (WGS). This process requires an [iron oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_oxide "Iron oxide") catalyst:[[116]](#cite_note-Oxtoby-116)

CO + H2O → CO2 + H2

Hydrogen is sometimes produced and consumed in the same industrial process, without being separated. In the [Haber process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haber_process "Haber process") for [ammonia production](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammonia_production "Ammonia production"), hydrogen is generated from natural gas.[[119]](#cite_note-119)

#### Partial oxidation of hydrocarbons

Other methods for CO and H2 production include partial oxidation of hydrocarbons:[[46]](#cite_note-uigi-46)

2 CH4 + O2 → 2 CO + 4 H2

Although less important commercially, coal can serve as a prelude to the above shift reaction:[[116]](#cite_note-Oxtoby-116)

C + H2O → CO + H2

[Olefin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olefin "Olefin") production units may produce substantial quantities of byproduct hydrogen, particularly from [cracking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petroleum_cracking "Petroleum cracking") light feedstocks like [ethane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethane "Ethane") or [propane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Propane "Propane").[[120]](#cite_note-120)

#### Water electrolysis

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cf/Hydrogen_production_via_Electrolysis.png/250px-Hydrogen_production_via_Electrolysis.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hydrogen_production_via_Electrolysis.png)

Inputs and outputs of the electrolysis of water production of hydrogen

[Electrolysis of water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrolysis_of_water "Electrolysis of water") is a conceptually simple method of producing hydrogen.

2 H2O(l) → 2 H2(g) + O2(g)

Commercial [electrolyzers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrolyzer "Electrolyzer") use [nickel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nickel "Nickel")-based catalysts in strongly alkaline solution. [Platinum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platinum "Platinum") is a better catalyst but is expensive.[[121]](#cite_note-121) The hydrogen created through electrolysis using renewable energy is commonly referred to as "[green hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_hydrogen "Green hydrogen")".[[122]](#cite_note-RoyalSociety-2021-122)

[Electrolysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrolysis "Electrolysis") of [brine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brine "Brine") to yield [chlorine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chlorine "Chlorine")[[123]](#cite_note-123) also produces high-purity hydrogen as a co-product, which is used for a variety of transformations such as [hydrogenations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogenation "Hydrogenation").[[124]](#cite_note-124)

The electrolysis process is more expensive than producing hydrogen from methane without [carbon capture and storage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_capture_and_storage "Carbon capture and storage").[[125]](#cite_note-Evans-2020-125)

Innovation in [hydrogen electrolyzers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_electrolyzer "Hydrogen electrolyzer") could make large-scale production of hydrogen from electricity more cost-competitive.[[126]](#cite_note-126)

#### Methane pyrolysis

Hydrogen can be produced by [pyrolysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrolysis "Pyrolysis") of [natural gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_gas "Natural gas") (methane), producing hydrogen gas and solid carbon with the aid of a catalyst and 74 [kJ/mol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joule_per_mole "Joule per mole") input heat:

CH4(g) → C(s) + 2 H2(g) (Δ*H*° = 74 kJ/mol)

The carbon may be sold as a manufacturing feedstock or fuel, or landfilled. This route could have a lower carbon footprint than existing hydrogen production processes, but mechanisms for removing the carbon and preventing it from reacting with the catalyst remain obstacles for industrial-scale use.[[127]](#cite_note-127): 17[[128]](#cite_note-128)

#### Thermochemical

[Water splitting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_splitting "Water splitting") is the process by which water is decomposed into its components. Relevant to the biological scenario is this equation:

2 H2O → 4 H+ + O2 + 4 e−

The reaction occurs in the [light-dependent reactions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light-dependent_reactions "Light-dependent reactions") in all [photosynthetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthetic "Photosynthetic") organisms. A few organisms, including the alga *[Chlamydomonas reinhardtii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chlamydomonas_reinhardtii "Chlamydomonas reinhardtii")* and [cyanobacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyanobacteria "Cyanobacteria"), have evolved a second step in the [dark reactions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_reaction "Dark reaction") in which protons and electrons are reduced to form H2 gas by specialized [hydrogenases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogenase "Hydrogenase") in the [chloroplast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chloroplast "Chloroplast").[[129]](#cite_note-129)

Efforts have been undertaken to [genetically modify](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetically_modify "Genetically modify") cyanobacterial hydrogenases to more efficiently generate H2 gas even in the presence of oxygen.[[130]](#cite_note-130) Efforts have also been undertaken with genetically‐modified alga in a [bioreactor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bioreactor "Bioreactor").[[131]](#cite_note-131)

Relevant to the thermal water-splitting scenario is this simple equation:

2 H2O → 2 H2 + O2

Over 200 thermochemical cycles can be used for [water splitting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_splitting "Water splitting"). Many of these cycles such as the [iron oxide cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_oxide_cycle "Iron oxide cycle"), [cerium(IV) oxide–cerium(III) oxide cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceria_based_thermochemical_cycles "Ceria based thermochemical cycles"), [zinc–zinc oxide cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zinc–zinc_oxide_cycle "Zinc–zinc oxide cycle"), [sulfur–iodine cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfur–iodine_cycle "Sulfur–iodine cycle"), [copper–chlorine cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copper–chlorine_cycle "Copper–chlorine cycle") and [hybrid sulfur cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hybrid_sulfur_cycle "Hybrid sulfur cycle") have been evaluated for their commercial potential to produce hydrogen and oxygen from water and heat without using electricity.[[132]](#cite_note-132) A number of labs (including in [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France"), [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany"), [Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greece "Greece"), [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan"), and the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States")) are developing thermochemical methods to produce hydrogen from solar energy and water.[[133]](#cite_note-133)

### Natural routes

#### Biohydrogen

Further information: [Biohydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biohydrogen "Biohydrogen")

H2 is produced in organisms by enzymes called [hydrogenases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogenase "Hydrogenase"). This process allows the host organism to use [fermentation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermentation "Fermentation") as a source of energy.[[134]](#cite_note-134) These same enzymes also can [oxidize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxidize "Oxidize") H2, such that the host organisms can subsist by reducing oxidized substrates using electrons extracted from H2.[[135]](#cite_note-135)

Hydrogenase enzymes feature [iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron "Iron") or [iron–nickel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron–nickel_alloy "Iron–nickel alloy") centers at their [active sites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Active_site "Active site").[[136]](#cite_note-136) The natural cycle of hydrogen production and consumption by organisms is called the [hydrogen cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_cycle "Hydrogen cycle").[[137]](#cite_note-Rhee6-137)

Some bacteria such as *[Mycobacterium smegmatis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycobacterium_smegmatis "Mycobacterium smegmatis")* can use the small amount of hydrogen in the atmosphere as a source of energy when other sources are lacking. Their hydrogenases feature small channels that exclude oxygen from the active site, permitting the reaction to occur even though the hydrogen concentration is very low and the oxygen concentration is as in normal air.[[108]](#cite_note-Grinter-108)[[138]](#cite_note-138)

Confirming the existence of hydrogenase‐employing microbes [in the human gut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_gut_flora "Human gut flora"), H2 occurs in human breath. The concentration in the breath of fasting people at rest is typically under 5 [parts per million](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parts_per_million "Parts per million") (ppm), but can reach 50 ppm when people with intestinal disorders consume molecules they cannot absorb during diagnostic [hydrogen breath tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_breath_test "Hydrogen breath test").[[139]](#cite_note-139)

#### Serpentinization

[Serpentinization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serpentinization "Serpentinization") is a geological mechanism which produces highly-[reducing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reduction_(chemistry) "Reduction (chemistry)") conditions.[[140]](#cite_note-FrostBeard2007-140) Under these conditions, water is capable of oxidizing [ferrous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferrous_ion "Ferrous ion") (Fe2+  
) ions in [fayalite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fayalite "Fayalite"), generating hydrogen gas:[[141]](#cite_note-Dincer-2015-141)[[142]](#cite_note-142)

Fe2SiO4 + H2O → 2 Fe3O4 + SiO2 + H2

Closely related to this geological process is the [Schikorr reaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schikorr_reaction "Schikorr reaction"):

3 Fe(OH)2 → Fe3O4 + 2 H2O + H2

This process also is relevant to the corrosion of [iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron "Iron") and [steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steel "Steel") in [oxygen-free](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anoxic_waters "Anoxic waters") [groundwater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groundwater "Groundwater") and in [reducing soils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reducing_soil "Reducing soil") below the [water table](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_table "Water table").[[143]](#cite_note-143)

### Laboratory syntheses

H2 is produced in laboratory settings, such as in the small-scale [electrolysis of water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrolysis_of_water "Electrolysis of water") using metal [electrodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrodes "Electrodes") and water containing an [electrolyte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrolyte "Electrolyte"), which liberates hydrogen gas at the [cathode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathode "Cathode"):[[97]](#cite_note-housecroft-97)

2H+(aq) + 2 e− → H2(g)

Hydrogen is also often a by-product of other reactions. Many metals react with water to produce H2, but the rate of hydrogen evolution depends on the metal, the pH, and the presence of alloying agents. Most often, hydrogen evolution is induced by acids. The [alkali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkali_earth_metals "Alkali earth metals") and [alkaline earth metals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkaline_earth_metals "Alkaline earth metals") as well as [aluminium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium "Aluminium"), [zinc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zinc "Zinc"), [manganese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese "Manganese"), and [iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron "Iron"), react readily with aqueous acids.[[97]](#cite_note-housecroft-97)

Zn + 2 H+ → Zn2+ + H2

Many metals, such as aluminium, are slow to react with water because they form [passivated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passivation_(chemistry) "Passivation (chemistry)") oxide coatings. An alloy of aluminium and [gallium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium "Gallium"), however, does react with water. In high-pH solutions, aluminium can react with  H2:[[97]](#cite_note-housecroft-97)

2 Al + 6 H2O + 2 OH− → 2 [Al(OH)4]− + 3 H2

### Storage

If H2 is to be used as an energy source, its storage is important. It dissolves only poorly in solvents. For example, at [room temperature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Room_temperature "Room temperature") and 0.1 [millipascals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pascal_(unit) "Pascal (unit)") (9.9×10−10 [atm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmosphere_(unit) "Atmosphere (unit)")), approx. 0.05 [moles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mole_(unit) "Mole (unit)") of hydrogen dissolve into one kilogram (2.2 lb) of [diethyl ether](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diethyl_ether "Diethyl ether").[[88]](#cite_note-UllmannH2-88) H2 can be stored in compressed form, although compressing costs energy. Liquefaction is impractical given hydrogen's low [critical temperature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critical_temperature "Critical temperature"). In contrast, ammonia and many hydrocarbons can be liquified at room temperature under pressure. For these reasons, hydrogen *carriers*—materials that reversibly bind H2—have attracted much attention. The key question is then the weight percent of H2-equivalents within the carrier material. For example, hydrogen can be reversibly absorbed into many [rare earths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rare_earths "Rare earths") and [transition metals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transition_metal "Transition metal")[[144]](#cite_note-Takeshita-144) and is soluble in both nanocrystalline and [amorphous metals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amorphous_metal "Amorphous metal").[[145]](#cite_note-Kirchheim1-145) Hydrogen [solubility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solubility "Solubility") in metals is influenced by local distortions or impurities in the [crystal lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal_lattice "Crystal lattice").[[146]](#cite_note-Kirchheim2-146) These properties may be useful when hydrogen is purified by passage through hot [palladium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palladium "Palladium") disks, but the gas's high solubility is also a metallurgical problem, contributing to the [embrittlement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_embrittlement "Hydrogen embrittlement") of many metals,[[147]](#cite_note-Rogers_1999_1057–1064-147) complicating the design of pipelines and storage tanks.[[148]](#cite_note-Christensen-148)

The most problematic aspect of metal hydrides for storage is their modest H2 content, often on the order of 1%. For this reason, there is interest in storage of H2 in compounds of low [molecular weight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molecular_weight "Molecular weight"). For example, [ammonia borane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammonia_borane "Ammonia borane") (H3N−BH3) contains 19.8 [weight percent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weight_percent "Weight percent") of H2. The problem with this material is that after release of H2, the resulting boron nitride does not re-add H2: i.e., ammonia borane is an irreversible hydrogen carrier.[[149]](#cite_note-149) More attractive are [hydrocarbons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrocarbon "Hydrocarbon") such as [tetrahydroquinoline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetrahydroquinoline "Tetrahydroquinoline"), which reversibly release some H2 when heated in the presence of a catalyst:[[150]](#cite_note-150)

C9H10NH ⇌ C9H7N + 2 H2

## Applications

See also: [Hydrogen economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_economy "Hydrogen economy")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/77/2023-10-19_Clean_Hydrogen_Ladder_5.0.png/500px-2023-10-19_Clean_Hydrogen_Ladder_5.0.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2023-10-19_Clean_Hydrogen_Ladder_5.0.png)

Hydrogen Ladder: Ranking of hydrogen applications and uses in the medium term, but analysts disagree[[151]](#cite_note-151)

### Petrochemical industry

Large quantities of H2 are used in the "upgrading" of [fossil fuels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fossil_fuels "Fossil fuels"). Key consumers of H2 include [hydrodesulfurization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrodesulfurization "Hydrodesulfurization") and [hydrocracking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrocracking "Hydrocracking"). Many of these reactions can be classified as [hydrogenolysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogenolysis "Hydrogenolysis"), i.e., the cleavage of bonds by hydrogen. Illustrative is the separation of [sulfur from liquid fossil fuels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweetening_(fossil_fuels) "Sweetening (fossil fuels)"):[[114]](#cite_note-KO-114)[[152]](#cite_note-UllmannHuse-152)

R2S + 2 H2 → H2S + 2 RH

### Hydrogenation

[Hydrogenation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogenation "Hydrogenation"), the addition of H2 to various substrates, is done on a large scale. Hydrogenation of N2 produces ammonia by the [Haber process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haber_process "Haber process"):[[152]](#cite_note-UllmannHuse-152)

N2 + 3 H2 → 2 NH3

This process consumes a few percent of the energy budget in the entire industry and is the biggest consumer of hydrogen. The resulting ammonia is used extensively in [fertilizer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fertilizer "Fertilizer") production; these fertilizers have become essential feedstocks in modern agriculture.[[153]](#cite_note-Smil_2004_Enriching-153) Hydrogenation is also used to convert [unsaturated fats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unsaturated_fat "Unsaturated fat") and [oils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vegetable_oil "Vegetable oil") to saturated fats and oils. The major application is the production of [margarine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margarine "Margarine"). [Methanol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methanol "Methanol") is produced by hydrogenation of carbon dioxide; the mixture of hydrogen and carbon monooxide used for this process is known as [syngas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syngas "Syngas").[[154]](#cite_note-154): 3.1 H2 is also used as a [reducing agent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reducing_agent "Reducing agent") for the conversion of some [ores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ore "Ore") to the metals.[[155]](#cite_note-155)[[97]](#cite_note-housecroft-97)

### Fuel

The potential for using hydrogen (H2) as a fuel has been widely discussed. Hydrogen can be used in [fuel cells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuel_cells "Fuel cells") to produce electricity,[[156]](#cite_note-156) or burned to generate heat.[[157]](#cite_note-Lewis-2021-157) When hydrogen is consumed in fuel cells, the only emission at the point of use is water vapor.[[157]](#cite_note-Lewis-2021-157) When burned, hydrogen produces relatively little pollution at the point of combustion, but can lead to thermal formation of harmful [nitrogen oxides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NOx "NOx").[[157]](#cite_note-Lewis-2021-157)

If hydrogen is produced with low or zero greenhouse gas emissions ([green hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_hydrogen "Green hydrogen")), it can play a significant role in decarbonizing energy systems where there are challenges and limitations to replacing fossil fuels with direct use of electricity.[[158]](#cite_note-IPCC-2022-158)[[125]](#cite_note-Evans-2020-125)

Hydrogen fuel can produce the intense heat required for industrial production of steel, cement, glass, and chemicals, thus contributing to the decarbonization of industry alongside other technologies, such as [electric arc furnaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_arc_furnace "Electric arc furnace") for steelmaking.[[159]](#cite_note-159) However, it is likely to play a larger role in providing industrial feedstock for cleaner production of ammonia and organic chemicals.[[158]](#cite_note-IPCC-2022-158) For example, in [steelmaking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steelmaking "Steelmaking"), hydrogen could function as a clean fuel and also as a low-carbon catalyst, replacing coal-derived [coke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coke_(fuel) "Coke (fuel)") (carbon):[[160]](#cite_note-160)

2FeO + C → 2Fe + CO2

vs

FeO + H2 → Fe + H2O

Hydrogen used to decarbonize transportation is likely to find its largest applications in shipping, aviation and, to a lesser extent, heavy goods vehicles, through the use of hydrogen-derived synthetic fuels such as [ammonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_ammonia "Green ammonia") and [methanol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_methanol "Green methanol") and fuel cell technology.[[158]](#cite_note-IPCC-2022-158) For light-duty vehicles including cars, hydrogen is far behind other [alternative fuel vehicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_fuel_vehicle "Alternative fuel vehicle"), especially compared with the rate of adoption of [battery electric vehicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battery_electric_vehicles "Battery electric vehicles"), and may not play a significant role in future.[[161]](#cite_note-161)

[![A black inverted funnel with blue glow emerging from its opening.](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/Shuttle_Main_Engine_Test_Firing_cropped_edited_and_reduced.jpg/250px-Shuttle_Main_Engine_Test_Firing_cropped_edited_and_reduced.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Shuttle_Main_Engine_Test_Firing_cropped_edited_and_reduced.jpg)

A [Space Shuttle Main Engine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Main_Engine "Space Shuttle Main Engine") burns hydrogen with oxygen, producing a nearly invisible flame at full thrust.

[Liquid hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_hydrogen "Liquid hydrogen") and [liquid oxygen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_oxygen "Liquid oxygen") together serve as [cryogenic propellants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryogenic_propellant "Cryogenic propellant") in [liquid-propellant rockets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid-propellant_rocket "Liquid-propellant rocket"), as in the [Space Shuttle main engines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_main_engines "Space Shuttle main engines"). [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") has investigated the use of [rocket propellant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocket_propellant "Rocket propellant") made from atomic hydrogen, boron or carbon that is frozen into solid molecular hydrogen particles suspended in liquid helium. Upon warming, the mixture vaporizes to allow the atomic species to recombine, heating the mixture to high temperature.[[162]](#cite_note-162)

Hydrogen produced when there is a surplus of [variable renewable electricity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variable_renewable_electricity "Variable renewable electricity") could in principle be stored and later used to generate heat or to re-generate electricity.[[163]](#cite_note-163) It can be further transformed into [synthetic fuels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthetic_fuel "Synthetic fuel") such as [ammonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammonia "Ammonia") and [methanol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methanol "Methanol").[[164]](#cite_note-164) Disadvantages of hydrogen fuel include high costs of storage and distribution due to hydrogen's explosivity, its large volume compared to other fuels, and its tendency to [embrittle materials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_embrittlement "Hydrogen embrittlement").[[118]](#cite_note-Griffiths-20212-118) The economic disadvantage of distribution can be reduced by co-locating facilities that use hydrogen in mining industry hubs.[[165]](#cite_note-165)

### Nickel–hydrogen battery

The very long-lived, rechargeable [nickel–hydrogen battery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nickel–hydrogen_battery "Nickel–hydrogen battery") developed for satellite power systems uses pressurized gaseous H2.[[166]](#cite_note-166) The [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station"),[[167]](#cite_note-167) [Mars Odyssey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Mars_Odyssey "2001 Mars Odyssey")[[168]](#cite_note-168) and the [Mars Global Surveyor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars_Global_Surveyor "Mars Global Surveyor")[[169]](#cite_note-169) are equipped with nickel-hydrogen batteries. In the dark part of its orbit, the [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope "Hubble Space Telescope") is also powered by nickel-hydrogen batteries, which were finally replaced in May 2009,[[170]](#cite_note-170) more than 19 years after launch and 13 years beyond their design life.[[171]](#cite_note-171)

### Semiconductor industry

Hydrogen is employed in [semiconductor manufacturing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor_manufacturing "Semiconductor manufacturing") to saturate broken ("dangling") bonds of [amorphous silicon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amorphous_silicon "Amorphous silicon") and [amorphous carbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amorphous_carbon "Amorphous carbon"), which helps in stabilizing the materials' properties.[[172]](#cite_note-172) Hydrogen, introduced as an unintended side-effect of production, acts as a shallow [electron donor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron_donor "Electron donor") leading to [n-type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N-type_semiconductor "N-type semiconductor") conductivity in [ZnO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ZnO "ZnO"), with important uses in [transducers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transducers "Transducers") and [phosphors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosphors "Phosphors").[[173]](#cite_note-173)[[174]](#cite_note-174) Detailed analysis of ZnO and of [MgO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MgO "MgO") shows evidence of four and six-fold hydrogen multicentre bonds.[[175]](#cite_note-175) The [doping behavior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dopant_(semiconductor) "Dopant (semiconductor)") of hydrogen varies with material.[[176]](#cite_note-176)[[177]](#cite_note-177)

### Niche and evolving uses

Beyond than the uses mentioned above, hydrogen is used in smaller scales in the following applications:

* Shielding gas: Hydrogen is used as a [shielding gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shielding_gas "Shielding gas") in [welding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welding "Welding") methods such as [atomic hydrogen welding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_hydrogen_welding "Atomic hydrogen welding").[[178]](#cite_note-178)[[179]](#cite_note-179)
* Coolant: Hydrogen is used as a [coolant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coolant "Coolant") in large electrical generators due to its high [thermal conductivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermal_conductivity "Thermal conductivity") and low density.[[180]](#cite_note-180) The first [hydrogen-cooled turbogenerator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen-cooled_turbogenerator "Hydrogen-cooled turbogenerator") went into service using gaseous hydrogen as a coolant in the rotor and the stator in 1937 in [Dayton, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dayton,_Ohio "Dayton, Ohio").[[181]](#cite_note-181)
* Cryogenic research: Liquid H2 is used in [cryogenic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryogenic "Cryogenic") research, including [superconductivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superconductivity "Superconductivity") studies.[[182]](#cite_note-182)
* Food industry: Hydrogen is an authorized [food additive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_additive "Food additive") ([E949](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E_number#E900–E999_(glazing_agents,_gases_and_sweeteners) "E number"))[[183]](#cite_note-183) that is used as a packaging gas,[[184]](#cite_note-184) and also has [antioxidant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioxidant "Antioxidant") properties.[[185]](#cite_note-185)
* Leak detection: Pure or mixed with nitrogen (sometimes called [forming gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forming_gas "Forming gas")), hydrogen is a [tracer gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracer_gas "Tracer gas") for [detection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leak_detection "Leak detection") of minute leaks. Applications can be found in the automotive, chemical, power generation, aerospace, and telecommunications industries;[[186]](#cite_note-186) it also allows for leak testing in food packaging.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

* Neutron moderation: [Deuterium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deuterium "Deuterium") (hydrogen-2) is used in [nuclear fission applications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CANDU_reactor "CANDU reactor") as a [moderator to slow neutrons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_moderator "Neutron moderator").[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]
* Nuclear fusion fuel: Deuterium is used in [nuclear fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_fusion "Nuclear fusion") reactions.[[8]](#cite_note-nbb-8)
* Isotopic labeling: Deuterium compounds have applications in chemistry and biology in studies of [isotope effects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinetic_isotope_effect "Kinetic isotope effect") on reaction rates.[[187]](#cite_note-187)

* Tritium uses: [Tritium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tritium "Tritium") (hydrogen-3), produced in [nuclear reactors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_reactor "Nuclear reactor"), is used in the production of [hydrogen bombs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_bomb "Hydrogen bomb"),[[188]](#cite_note-188) as an isotopic label in the biosciences,[[31]](#cite_note-holte-31) and as a source of [beta radiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_radiation "Beta radiation") in [radioluminescent paint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tritium_radioluminescence "Tritium radioluminescence") for instrument dials and emergency signage.[[26]](#cite_note-Traub95-26)

Chemical compound

In hydrogen pipelines and steel storage vessels, hydrogen molecules are prone to reacting with metals, causing [hydrogen embrittlement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_embrittlement "Hydrogen embrittlement") and leaks in the pipeline or storage vessel.[[190]](#cite_note-Li-2022-190) Since it is lighter than air, hydrogen does not easily accumulate to form a combustible gas mixture.[[190]](#cite_note-Li-2022-190) However, even without ignition sources, high-pressure hydrogen leakage may cause spontaneous combustion and [detonation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detonation "Detonation").[[190]](#cite_note-Li-2022-190)

Hydrogen is flammable when mixed even in small amounts with air. Ignition can occur at a [volumetric ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volumetric_ratio "Volumetric ratio") of hydrogen to air as low as 4%.[[191]](#cite_note-191) In approximately 70% of hydrogen ignition accidents, the ignition source cannot be determined.[[190]](#cite_note-Li-2022-190)

Hydrogen fire, while being extremely hot, is almost invisible to the human eye, and thus can lead to accidental burns.[[45]](#cite_note-spinoff-2016-45) Hydrogen is non-toxic,[[192]](#cite_note-192) but like most gases [it can cause asphyxiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inert_gas_asphyxiation "Inert gas asphyxiation") in the absence of adequate ventilation.[[193]](#cite_note-193)
